Patterns and Parallels

☙ ❧

This section compares Rolo’s wonders with their sources, traces the word shine, and sets out five accounts of the novel’s events.

In Dark Shine, Rolo Danovitz and his Group build a new world that collapses within thirty days. The title phrase acquires its meanings in Chapters Two, Three, Eight, and Nine, and conflicting speakers and reports give rival accounts of what is real. In Chapter Eleven, Rolo is identified as the Second Beast.

Testing the Wonders

Rolo’s project draws on mathematical invention, fairy-tale enchantment, and distorted biblical promises. The table sets each of its wonders beside a real-world or biblical reference point.

Reference point Parallel or contrast in the novel
Real world-expansion by many groups over centuries; several hundred past, several dozen active (Bart’s memo, Ch. 4). Rolo’s particular “trigger move” of two hundred million hectares, run on “the gyroscopy of a tightening spiral” that BAM calculates cannot sustain itself past thirty days.
Mathematical discovery through discussion, dreaming, and receptivity to ideas (Brendan, Ch. 2). Rolo directs Brendan’s algebra reading; Beth supplies fairy tales with their endings marked out. Opium-laced snuff accompanies the dream (Ch. 2).
Brendan speculates that gold pours from fissures as the earth expands (Ch. 2). Fairy gold that turns on waking into iron clinkers, duck feathers, and goat manure (Ch. 2).
Rolo insists, “There is always a bottom,” and says his father lives below the crust (Ch. 6). A city built on a crust with “no bottom under it” (Norbert, Ch. 6).
Uaireanta, or Sometimes Valley: the changing valley of O’Crocker’s tale (Ch. 2). Spacious City: the new metropolis and popular name for the wider Accrual project. Like the dream-valley, it is beautiful and unstable.
The moon as a measure of time. Beth says the moon has been absent through the first twenty-eight days (Ch. 9). The city begins to collapse on the twenty-ninth night; the retreat starts on the thirtieth morning.
Real people with continuous identity. “New people” who appear during the fifty-second transition and “honestly didn’t have very clear ideas of just who they were” (Ch. 5); unidentifiable corpses at every quake site.
Matthew 16:13–17: Jesus asks who people say he is; Peter confesses; Jesus attributes that revelation to the Father. Rolo asks the question of himself and answers himself: Scion of Dan, King of Babylon, triple cube (Ch. 9).
“Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58): the divine name and pre-existence. “Before Beelzebub was, I am!” Rolo claims priority within the demonic order (Ch. 11).
“I will come again” (John 14:3): the Parousia. “I will come again, with more substance, when I am older.” Title of Chapter Eleven: “Till I Come Back.”
Psalm 127:1 (Vulgate 126:1): the Lord builds the house and guards the city. The Latin is “Nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum” and “Nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem.” Title of Chapter Nine: “Is the City Built and the Lord Has Not Built It?” Rolo’s “father lives down there,” below the crust.
The Eucharist: “do this in memory of me.” A cult asks Rolo to leave “token blood” of something killed in great pain as a memento till he returns (Ch. 10).

The novel distinguishes destructive enchantment from real foundations, though Felicity’s arguments for love and the temporary reality of projected matter allow artificial things some value of their own. Members of the Group also disagree about what they have made; Norbert warns that the city has no bottom under it.

Tart and the Language of Shine

The word monkeyshine connects the I-Forget Bird’s warning with Tart’s responses, which move from alarm to fascination and finally to a plan to trap Rolo. Norbert’s gold memo in Chapter Three and Rolo’s third face in Chapter Eight add further senses of the title phrase.

  • Ch. 2, the I-Forget Bird. The rook warns Brendan: “It is a Monkeyshine, it is a Kinderschein, it is a dark shine.” The title phrase first appears here.
  • Ch. 2, Tart. After repeated expulsions, she calls from a window, though the Group does not hear her: “What you are starting on now is a monkeyshine, a Rolo Danovitz monkeyshine or wonder-boy shine.” She adds, “I understand that now.”
  • Ch. 4, Tart inside the world-switch. Watching the expansion in suspended time, she says, “This is the monkeyshine, the dirty trick, the dirty shine.”
  • Ch. 7, Tart’s Letter from Prison, earlier passage. “This is a monkey-shine, this is a damned putto-shine, this is a mirage-shine, and it is a dark and slimy trick.”
  • Ch. 7, Tart’s Letter from Prison, later passage. “It is all a monkey-shine or a Rolo-shine and it can’t last. But I don’t want it stopped. I want to see how it works out.”
  • Ch. 11, Tart tracking Rolo. She plans to use Rolo’s weakness for shines against him: “I will play on his weakness for shines, for monkey-shines and boy-shines and devil-shines. We will trap him in a shine.”

Five Overlapping Framings

The novel gives five accounts of the same events, drawn from genetics, infernal power, classical mythology, science, and espionage. The narrator says the three impact studies in Chapter Nine are correct in their estimates, although their writers disagree about what the disaster means.

Framing What the Group is What Rolo is In-book source
I. Genetic A group with engineered inheritances, extraordinary abilities, and preterhuman longevity. An eleven-year-old superchild who combines Raingold genetics and Noonan illusion-craft. Norbert Hardcore’s inheritance memo (Ch. 1); Bart’s iceberg memo (Ch. 4).
II. Infernal Rolo and his associates have dealings with infernal authorities; their origins and fates differ. A being who describes his nature as human and diabolical, one of a rare devil’s dozen. His superior warns that failure sets their project back a hundred or a thousand years. Principality-animal-spirit scene (Ch. 11); Rolo’s “father lives down there” (Ch. 6); Beth sent to command an Iron Hundred in Hell (Ch. 11).
III. Olympian The returning Olympians in Maniple’s interpretation, opposed by the Consortium as Titans. According to Maniple’s report, the original putto: an indwelt bronze statue-boy born in Hephaestus’s furnace. Maniple impact study (Ch. 9); Chrona as Venus; the Titan/Olympian frame around the Consortium battle.
IV. Scientific The Hobgoblin Report interprets the mythological conflict as human arrogance and uncorrected science. A destructive human undertaking enlarged into myth, in that report’s account. Hobgoblin Report, by Raymond Bunko, Karen Kvikmand, and Curtis H. Goblin (Ch. 9).
V. Espionage A threat investigated by BAM/SNUFF and targeted through the Contract Man’s network; Nelly’s possible handler is not identified. The “Destroyer of the World,” eleven years old, passing today into a new and invulnerable stage, with a twenty-year fuse to world-destruction. BAM (Chs. 1, 4); the Contract Man’s deposition and the Tellurian Institute’s observation of the final trap (Ch. 11).

The Book in Story-Time

☙ ❧

This section sets out the order of events and examines the figure of Rolo, the hidden-room device, the Seventh Equation episode, and the ending.

§ 1The Chronology

The main action runs over thirty days, but recollections, foundation papers, and delayed reports interrupt it. Chapters One and Two precede the transition; Chapter Three inserts background memos; Chapter Four includes surveillance history and the dawn flight. The BAMs arrive just as the Rolo Group begins its flight, with Rolo expected to land thirty-eight seconds later. BAM witnesses the expansion in distorted time and is captured before the narration follows the Group into the new world.

Ch. Story time What happens
1 Night before the switch (old world) The Group returns from the Outer Winds Area. Tart questions them and copies Norbert’s inheritance memo. In his closing “Dog Robber” memo, Norbert sees the influences of Rolo’s grandfather and great-grandmother in the boy.
2 That same night Brendan’s ritual. He lays out seven snuff piles “in honor of the seven dreams,” at least one of which is taken by a non-human visitor he later cannot account for. He enters the embedded O’Crocker fairy tale and takes the Seventh Equation from the I-Forget Bird. Tart is at the mansion, thrown out of the room three times and returning three times; she calls from a window that what they are doing is a monkeyshine, but the Group does not hear her.
3 Background before the transition Foundation papers on expansion, gold, love and hatred, and the ancientness of new things set out the theory behind the transformation.
4 Dawn: the fifty-second transition Two flights at once. The Rolo Group boards their hover-craft; the BAM quintet (Art, Bart, Hart, Dart, Tart) boards theirs. The BAMs arrive “just at the moment when the Rolo Group began its own flight” and land first. The Rolo Group will land thirty-eight seconds later. The BAMs, in suspended time, watch an expansion “in the act of happening.” Cheerful, “exuberant” creatures from the expansion put iron manacles on Tart’s wrists and take the quintet “to the pokey.” Tart, inside the transition, names what is happening: “this is the monkeyshine, the dirty trick, the dirty shine.”
5 Day 1 of Spacious City The new world comes up around the landings. Fifty thousand earthquakes in fifty seconds. Unidentifiable corpses at each quake site. “New people” who arrive with unclear identities.
6 Early days; opens probably on the second morning Court life, the magicians, Chróna’s politics, the hidden-room device, and the Dead Dogs. The BAMs are freed early in the city’s life. Rolo tells Norbert that his father lives below the crust.
7 Interlude (document dump) One Letter from Prison, written before Tart’s release but entered into the record afterward. The narrative says closer contact with the Group later edited her mind. Within that letter she moves from warning to wanting to see the project continue. The chapter also presents the Outer Winds Area Mirages investigation.
8 Later in the city’s life The tide begins to turn. Norbert Hardcore starts separating from the Group. Rolo’s third face, the face of “Holy Deception,” appears.
9 Days 28–29, continuing to predawn Beth notices the absent moon after twenty-eight days; Nelly cannot remember it. Three impact studies assess the world-change. Rolo announces his identity and plans. The SHINE dictionary entry occurs here, p. 126. Collapse begins at nightfall of the twenty-ninth day; snakes fall before dawn.
10 Thirtieth morning and the retreat The Group frees the hover-craft, Rolo kills Brendan for the cult’s blood token, and the survivors retreat through Wittenberg, Dresden, Munich, Bern, Milano, Arles, and Boulogne. The reports embedded here offer conflicting appraisals of the disaster.
11 Continuation of the retreat and final afternoon Rolo meets infernal associates. Chróna is branded and sold; Beth accepts command of an Iron Hundred in Hell. Tart uses residues of Norbert, Felicity, and Hornblende to enter the hidden-room network. After Rolo’s animal ordeal, she obtains flesh from his severed shoulder and strengthens her access. Five boys pin him in frog form while observers at the Tellurian Institute watch. The novel ends with a coin flip proposed and Rolo’s fate undecided.

§ 2The Figure of Rolo

Rolo has overlapping genetic, mythological, infernal, and political identities. The entries below draw on his family history, his own speeches, and the reports of those who observe him.

The bronze figure

Maniple’s Chapter Nine impact study places Rolo’s birth in Hephaestus’s furnace and calls him “the original putto or indwelt statue-boy.” This bronze origin connects him with the Putti of the legend in Chapter Four, who are brilliant and short-lived. In art, a putto is a small boy figure, often winged.

The genetic construction

Norbert’s Chapter One memo gives the engineered genealogy. Rolo’s maternal grandfather is the genetic tamperer Rolo Raingold; his paternal grandfather is the illusionist Numerology Noonan. His father Nathaniel Noonan is a genetic engineer, and Chróna is also a product of genetic tampering.

The devil’s dozen and the father below

A being described as principality, animal, and spirit tells Rolo that his father was furious and that failure sets their work back a hundred years or a thousand. Rolo describes his own nature as human and diabolical, one of a devil’s dozen (p. 148). Chróna’s sale and Beth’s command of an Iron Hundred in Hell show that infernal powers stand behind the Group’s adventure.

The House of Dan

Rolo calls himself the scion of the House of Dan and King of Babylon (Ch. 9). Chapter Eight quotes Rev. P. Huchede on Antichrist’s possible Danite origin, Babylonian birth, and education by magicians (p. 105). Earlier parallels include Irenaeus, Against Heresies V.30.2, on Jeremiah 8:16 and Dan’s omission from Revelation’s sealed tribes, and Hippolytus, On Christ and Antichrist 14–15, on Dan’s lion and serpent imagery. Rolo’s snake imagery corresponds to the serpent of Dan in Hippolytus; his name Dolg the Dagger may also belong to this tradition.

The King of Babylon

Chróna explains the archaeological club whose members give birth at Babylon so their children may be proclaimed its king; she also insists Rolo’s kingship has a deeper meaning. Rolo’s title connects Spacious City and its king with Babylon, the corrupt city of Revelation. Chróna’s branding and sale recall both the harlot’s degradation in Revelation 17:16 and the trade in human beings condemned in Revelation 18:13.

“Who do men say that I am?”

Rolo borrows the question from “the Other” and answers it himself with Dan, Babylon, and geometric titles (Ch. 9, p. 124). In Matthew 16:13–17, Peter confesses Jesus’s identity and Jesus credits the Father’s revelation.

“Before Beelzebub was, I am”

“Before Beelzebub was, I am!” (Ch. 11) adapts John 8:58. Rolo replaces Abraham with a demonic name and claims pre-existence for himself.

Till I come back, and the twenty-year clock

Rolo calls the present adventure a rehearsal and promises to return with greater substance. The Contract Man warns that Rolo is passing into an invulnerable stage and that the world’s fuse will burn for about twenty years. A Tellurian observer says killing Rolo now would prevent his return and probably gain another canonical thousand years. Rolo’s superior likewise warns that failure sets their work back a hundred years or a thousand.

The third face

Rolo’s third face appears in Chapter Eight (pp. 108–109). He has already shown a beautiful face and an ugly one; the third is a face of deception. During the mutual adoration, Rolo wears a dark shine and his worshippers invoke “the holy deception.”

§ 3The Hidden-Room Network

In Chapter Six, Rolo tells Norbert something that shocks him: “There is a bottom below the crust that we are standing on. My father lives down there. We get echoes from that bottom, and it is not all that far below us. ‘There is always a bottom,’ that is the new guide-line. Not only that, but we have the secret in us of recognizing that bottom when we come to it.” Every Group member has a “hidden room” containing a “touch-stone” for identifying authentic reality. Extracted, it is the true reader: a device that would “analyze any part of the world, in time or in space, as to its authenticity.”

The BAM monitors discover the unscannable hidden rooms in Chapter Four. Freed early in the city’s life, the political prisoners report their finding, and the Group undertakes its own interior excavation in Chapter Six.

Rolo wants the touch-stone so the Group can find real ground while continuing to play fast and loose near its edges. Norbert resists the plan, and the true reader later fails.

The network in Chapter Eleven

In Chapter Six the device appears to be passive. In Chapter Eleven, Tart explains that it works in both directions and links its users. Her use of it brings about the ending:

“I track Rolo now by the ‘hidden room’ device that he once shared with other members of the Rolo Group, and now believes that he shares with nobody at all. But he shares it with me. I have been tracking Rolo all day by the dead bodies that he leaves behind him. I have gathered up still-living but last-gasp residues of Norbert Hardcore (who died bravely — but Oh so clumsily! — on the barricades of Spacious City), of Felicity Octave who was my friend and simpatica, of the elegant Hornblende Michaelson. By the remnants of these three, I am a partaker of the homing information of the ‘hidden room’ device. By this, I can come into Rolo and implant things in his mind. He believes in his own intuitions. If only he does not see my hand when I hand these to him, he will believe that they are his own.”

The hidden-room device links the Group’s members. Tart gains access through the surviving residues of Norbert, Felicity, and Hornblende. She uses that access to implant suggestions Rolo will mistake for his own intuitions.

The trap develops in two stages. Tart’s report describes her plan to invent a Hornblende memory praising the Green Groben Frog. After the Ordeal of the Animals, she obtains sinew and flesh from Rolo’s severed shoulder and uses them to supply the final thought and inclination. Tempted by the imagined elegance of the frog, Rolo transforms. The five boys have separately shared a dream, but its sender is never identified.

§ 4The Seventh Equation: Ritual, Fairy Tale, and Warning

Chapter Two combines mathematical discovery, a drug-assisted dream, fairy-tale travel, and a warning about a deceiver. The gathering and the sudden inspiration resemble Pentecost, but the opium, the concealed endings, and the warning about Rolo mark the revelation as a deceptive one.

Sevens and eights structure the episode. Brendan needs a seventh equation, lays out seven snuff piles, and seeks the seventh pass into the valley. Rolo later calls himself an eight-stage rocket with seven disposable boosters. In biblical usage seven signifies completion, and in Christian symbolism the eighth day signifies a new beginning. Rolo’s rocket image applies these numbers to the Group: he is the eighth stage, and his companions are the boosters to be discarded.

The gathering around the dream

Brendan lays out snuff “in honor of the seven dreams” and allows for visitors who may partake. He later remembers that some snuff-dipping visitors have escaped his memory. Seven dreamers appear again in Chapter Seven’s cave ideogram and Chapter Eight’s Seven Rugged Dreamers.

The sequence

1. Preparation for building. Rolo pushes Brendan to complete his mathematics while the Group, which does not hear Tart’s warning from the window, prepares to act on the equations.

2. Restricted reading. Rolo assigns Effinger’s algebra and withholds its resolutions; Beth supplies O’Crocker’s tales with their endings marked out. Brendan uses Poppycock Snuff, an apple, and an electrical tickler.

3. The dream journey. Brendan enters O’Crocker’s story of Dennis O’Day and climbs Toireasc Mountain toward the hidden seventh pass. The tale and his own dreaming become difficult to separate. The journey provides a mathematical solution and leaves a material residue when he wakes.

4. The bird. Brendan identifies the forgetful rook by exploiting its inability to remember the scouted berry thickets. Although it supplies the equation, the bird warns Brendan against Rolo.

5. The warning. The bird names the danger:

“What you are working on and who you are working for is as crooked as a snake that bends back to his starting point. This is he who will deceive if possible even the elect. It is a trap and a trick. It is a Monkeyshine, it is a Kinderschein, it is a dark shine.”

The phrase about deceiving even the elect comes from Matthew 24:24 and Mark 13:22. The snake that bends back to its starting point resembles an ouroboros; self-eating snakes appear later in the fires. Brendan goes ahead with the equation despite the warning.

The bird also tells Brendan to keep his apple so he can return; its seeds grow into the apple trees that mark his route home.

6. The valley. Through the seventh pass Brendan sees Uaireanta Valley in a golden aspect. Its appearance and era keep changing, which gives the Sometimes Valley its name. Like Spacious City, it is beautiful and unstable.

7. Return and residue. Brendan brings back the equation and a cap that held gold. When he wakes, the cap spills out an assortment of debris and refuse. Beth explains: “These are all the things that gold coins and gold nuggets turn into, in any of the cultures, when one wakes from an enchantment.”

§ 5The Frog, the Boys, and the Coin

At the end of the novel, Rolo, in the form of a bright green frog, is pinned under a forked stick, and five grubby boys argue about whether to kill him. By the accounts of the Contract Man and the Tellurian observers, the world’s survival depends on what they decide.

Tart’s counter-operation

Tart pursues several ways of killing Rolo, including contact with the Contract Man and the frog scheme, which she calls a fetish possibility. The Contract Man reports more than a hundred deaths among people who recognize the threat. With organized resistance failing, the boys are left as the last opportunity.

The boys’ part

“It must be done by boys. It cannot be done by adults, nor by females of any age. It cannot be done by myself.” By Tart’s rule for the fetish trap, only boys can complete it.

The watchers

The Tellurian Institute’s monitor picks up the most important event in the world, which is the boys and the frog. Its observers judge the scene correctly despite their afflictions, and then deride it. Much of the ending is given through their dialogue, and the narration supplies the final exclamation: “Aw, won’t they ever decide it!”

The unfinished decision

One boy proposes a coin flip; Tart urges him to search his pocket. The novel stops before the toss. If Rolo survives, his destructive return lies about twenty years ahead. If the boys kill him, the Tellurian observer expects another thousand years of reprieve.

By this point organized resistance has been compromised, and even Tart is briefly tempted to let Rolo go. The wolves and leopards judge him in the final ordeal, then acknowledge him.

Open Questions

☙ ❧

This section sets out six questions the novel leaves unresolved.

The novel leaves several relationships unresolved, and a number of recurring images connect scenes far apart in the book. The questions below concern these relationships and images.

I.The multiple infiltrations

Chapter Four identifies Felicity as a BAM plant whom Nelly believes she created, then asks who might have created or employed the equally synthetic Nelly. Tart openly monitors the Group, Felicity infiltrates it, and Nelly’s possible handler is never named. How does Nelly fit among the overlapping operations of BAM, the Contract Man’s network, and the Tellurian Institute?

II.The Seven Dreamers

Seven dreamers appear in Brendan’s seven snuff piles in Chapter Two, the cave ideogram in Chapter Seven, and the seven open-eyed dreamers discussed in Chapter Eight. Eustace’s cloud-oracle and Selma’s account of a widespread belief add further instances. Do these images refer to the same beings? How do the Dreamers relate to the Group and its work of creation?

III.The Wolves and the Leopards at four levels

The Wolves and Leopards appear as rival political parties, a folk drama, constellations in Maniple’s report, and judgment animals in Chapter Eleven. The last are called “the Judgements of the Father” and “the Judgement of the Father.” What joins these political, theatrical, cosmic, and infernal forms?

IV.Homo invisibilis

Bart’s Chapter Four memo develops the iceberg image of mostly invisible humanity and discusses homo invisibilis. His account of visibility as an extraordinarily narrow band of wave-lengths extends the novel’s doubts about what instruments and senses can detect. How does this invisible humanity relate to the Ninth Class and the people who appear during the world-shift?

V.Liturgical parallels

Several episodes correspond to the Christian sequence of Last Supper, Passion, Resurrection, and Pentecost. Chapter Eight’s cherry bowl and its epigraph from Matthew recall the betrayal at the Last Supper. Chapter Six, “Joy in the Morning,” and Chapter Two’s gathering around a dream may correspond to the Resurrection and Pentecost. How do these episodes connect with Rolo’s parody of the promised return?

VI.The politics of Spacious City

Spacious City fills almost at once with factions, militias, theaters, oracles, churches, and sporting institutions. Chróna’s Barefoot Barons, Gallowglass Guards, and Red-Faced Regulars use the city’s abundance to secure political control, while the Consortium brings a rival power into the city. How do the cultural flowering and the political order support each other, and where does that alliance begin to fail?

“This is not real, this is not real! I cannot cry out this warning often enough.”
Tart, from her prison letter, Chapter Seven

Chapter One: Earthquakes in May

pp. 1–17

“These have their way with me: / New Cities today, / Quails from the sky a-fall, / Earthquakes in May.”

Arrival of the Group

The eight members of the “Rolo Group” return to their town mansion after a stint in the “Outer Winds Area,” arriving with gusty winds, the rich-rattle of coins and nuggets, and minor earthquakes. They are met by Tart, a Cocked Eye Hit Guy from BAM (Benevolent Advisory Monitors), already waiting at the mansion to question their motives. Brendan explains that the premonitory quakes send “echoes of themselves, about eight hours into the past and eight hours into the future.”

The Motive Interview

Tart questions the Group’s publicity and motives. Brendan describes making a world the next morning and destroying the old one first: “We will destroy this world, and in fifty seconds we will build another one.”

Character Introductions

The core eight are Rolo, the eleven-year-old leader; Brendan, mathematician and magician; Beth, tactician; Chróna, archaeologist and Rolo’s mother; Norbert, the strong-arm; Hornblende, devoted to elegance; Nelly, involved in synthetic personhood; and Felicity, a synthetic recruit. Rolo shifts between beauty and ugliness, with cruelty beneath his childlike appearance.

Norbert’s Memo: Numerology Noonan

Norbert’s memo recounts three shows by Numerology Noonan at the Rialto Theatre: Friday night, Saturday matinee, and Saturday night. The final act appears to disembowel a farmer before 2,200 spectators. When the crowd becomes dangerous, Noonan drops the scene about three feet and the town disappears. Noonan insists the killing was real, then unsettles Norbert’s certainty about what was illusion and what was real. Norbert’s apparent forty-eight hours are said to have lasted seven minutes; the memo preserves his doubt about the body and the approaching animals.

Chapter Two: The Seventh Equation

pp. 18–29

“All things begin in order, so shall they end, and so shall they begin again. . .”

The Demand for Algebra

Rolo demands that Brendan Michaels finish the “Enabling Algebras” and the “Seventh Equation” required for the world-shift before he goes to sleep.

O’Crocker’s Tales

Beth gives Brendan O’Crocker’s Crock of Gold Tales with the endings marked out. Rolo separately directs him to Effinger’s algebra without its resolutions. Brendan enters the I-Forget Bird story in a dream to obtain the Seventh Equation.

The Dream Valley

Brendan enters the tale’s changing Uaireanta Valley, identifies the I-Forget Bird, and obtains the mathematical synthesis despite its warning about Rolo.

Waking with Gold

Brendan wakes with the equation. His cap spills cinders, clinkers, broken pottery, shells, feathers, and manure. He protests that it was gold when he started back. Beth replies: “These are all the things that gold coins and gold nuggets turn into, in any of the cultures, when one wakes from an enchantment.”

Philosophy of Building

Hornblende gives the “calling to build” speech: they will build cities, realms, sciences, arts, “deep piety and abiding grace,” and “even the smallest things monumentally,” for full people, quasi-people, wraiths, and trolls alike. Norbert breaks in to insist on “diamond hardness”: “hard as diamonds, hard as bearings, hard as hearts, hard as hell.” Nelly Mercury corrects him: bearings above a certain small size are “hard-soft, amenable, and self-lubricating.” Norbert concedes only that the largest bearings, “those of the poles of the universes,” are totally hard.

Chapter Three: Thus Is It Built

pp. 30–44

“How might one tell whether a thing grows, if it grows uniformly, and the measuring-sticks grow at the same time, and all its surroundings grow at the same rate?” (excerpt from Harold Buildingmaster, Worlds Without End)

Rolo’s Expansion Memo

Rolo outlines the project: intruding two hundred million hectares of “new land” into open use across approximately twenty thousand separate plots. This is a “trigger move” that will swing the balance into a new category. He discusses the “Lord of Unreality” and the “Westering Illusion,” noting that the common people are in “deep suspicion about these things.”

Fortean Weather Control

Rolo’s memo argues that below 7,000 meters everyone lives in a “Fortean Universe,” a low-air world subject to “Illusionist Influence, if only that influence is resolute enough.” Rainfall, weather, and most local phenomena are generated below this level, where the Group’s manipulations can take hold. Above 7,000 meters lie the strato-winds and “unremitting weather” that no one local can touch. Rolo notes parenthetically: “I seem to fit into a Fortean Universe better than The Other does.”

Norbert’s Gold Theory

Norbert’s memo sets out the theory of the “secret masters of the world”: they are very rich and they “stand behind the world and guarantee to pay the bills of the world.” Gold bleeds out of tectonic fractures as the world expands; almost none has been lost, and most is reburied in private vaults. “It is the reburied gold that gives the earth its obscure shine, its dark shine, the brightness of the ‘sun within’ that has been discovered on photographs of the Earth taken from Mars.” He argues that “a desert is a place where a great lot of hatred has been vented,” and that “the only magic in world-building, or in anything else, is truculence.”

Felicity’s Memo: Hatred and Love

Felicity quotes Rolo’s belief that hatred will generate the polarities needed by their motors. She rejects hate-based mathematics as regressive and insists on fondness, affection, and love, even if synthetic substitutes must initially stand in. “It is as difficult and as vital to make and expand a love as to make and expand a world.” The memo also records her fear that she is an artificial person and includes the recurring phrase about deceiving even the elect.

Brendan’s Memo: Ancientness of New Things

Brendan discusses “time-fabric” and the “intervals” between worlds. Every new thing arrives complete with fossils of itself. He asks whether time is a “flicker-fabric” made of intervals of nothing separated by intervals of something.

Chapter Four: Monitors of BAM

pp. 45–57

Opening sentence: “The activities of the Rolo Danovitz group did not go unobserved, else what are intelligence organizations for?”

Surveillance Apparatus

The “Cocked Eye BAM” (a sub-group of SNUFF, or Superview of Normalized Unitized Fact Forming) monitors the Rolo Group via brain-waves, dream transparencies, and “written-on air carbons” of their memos. They can lift brain-waves wirelessly to a distance of a thousand meters.

The Infiltrator Revealed

Felicity Octave is confirmed as a BAM creature and spy inside the Rolo Group, though Nelly Mercury believes she herself created Felicity. The Cocked Eyes have done “a little bit of implanting” in her. The chapter then asks whose creature Nelly Mercury is, since she is “at least as synthetic a person as is Felicity.”

Putto Hyper-Sapiens Classification

Rolo is classified as a “Putto Hyper-Sapiens,” a being of “dumbfounding mentality” who can shift between ugly and handsome from one viewing angle to the next. Dart cites a very old legend “in the most benighted nook of Italy” (with an “almost identical” parallel in the interior of Borneo): God created the Putti first of all and took their advice on creating the rest of the universe, but He set a very short life as the punishment for their bright intelligence. On the thirtieth night, the first Putti burned up like meteors. Half a dozen escaped by tampering with the number system and putting on ugly faces. Their hidden descendants still trick their way into being born to humans; they are brilliant and short-lived, and they introduce contradictions into the world.

The Hidden Room Exception

The monitors discover that all Rolo Group members share “hidden rooms” in their persons that cannot be scanned, interior caches containing a treasure. This is the first mention of the “hidden room device,” which the Group uncovers in Chapter Six.

The World-Shift

The monitors arrive in the “Outer Winds Area” just as the world shifts in fifty seconds. Monsters emerge, “pleasant, venturesome, exuberant, morning-bright” creatures who shackle the monitors. Time runs slow, then fast. Rolo’s first words to the new world: “Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased your father to give you a kingdom.”

Chapter Five: Early Times in Spacious City

pp. 58–73

“There is no such thing as absolute hallucination. There is no such thing as ‘mere’ group hypnosis.”

Arrival and Assessment

The Rolo Group lands on the “new planet” amid “victimless quakes” that kill unidentified people and leave strewn wreckage with no corresponding missing buildings. Fifty thousand earthquakes occur in fifty seconds, following the “seven year itch” cycle.

Spacious City Established

Rolo’s sign has two lines: “SPACIOUS CITY - Population 8.” and “GREATER METROPOLITAN AREA - Population 21,695,543.” The smaller figure identifies the initial Group; the larger anticipates growth. The new world or project is called Accrual, and Spacious City becomes its popular city-state name. The royal-court discussion develops in Chapter Six.

Megalithic Construction

The Group builds massive structures while in trance: the Hanging Gardens of Pleasure, a Pyramidal Cenotaph, the Tower of the People (a live data bank with life-sized replicas of all citizens). Construction happens faster than consciousness can track.

The Ninth Class

Arutinov’s account names the Aoratoi kai Anarithmoi, the Invisible and Uncountable Ones. Loud, adaptable, and frequently overlooked, they bring rapid shifts of population and opinion. The chapter speculates that more than half the world’s people belong to this ninth class.

Sudden Cultural Flowering

The SCF (Sudden Cultural Flowering) begins: five metropolitan newspapers (the Joyful Journal, the Fountain, the Daily Declarer, the Ram’s Horn, and the Morning Rooster), Haiku Drawings of seventeen strokes, Hundred Word Essays, and the “No Dramas,” street plays in which an “Idiot Child” spins and selects actors from the crowd.

Chapter Six: Joy in the Morning

pp. 74–89

“We who are born into the world’s artificial system can never adequately know how little in our present state and circumstance is natural, and how much is merely the interpolation of the perverted mind and heart of man.” (excerpt from Hawthorne, “The New Adam and Eve”)

Political Prisoners

Rolo frees the five BAM monitors (Art, Bart, Hart, Dart, Tart) and makes league with them. They report that much of what Rolo’s people regarded as “normal” was already expansion conditions brought about by groups working for decades or centuries. “They weren’t building on natural earth. They were building on already contrived earth.”

Court of Magicians

Brendan questions Alembic Nicholas about conjured food, arguing that the food he orders from Happy Harry is evidence of a preferred reality. Alembic answers that Harry is simply a better magician in that field. Their debate turns to the relative charges and capacitance of different realities. Brendan worries about his own continuing identity and validity as he moves among them.

Chróna’s Corruption

Chróna holds court with “chthonic” friends: spirits-of-the-earth people, the novo intelligents, novo rich, and novo instigators. Political and fiscal corruption grows “tall and strong in less than a handful of days.” Her party, the Barefoot Barons, and militias (Red-Faced Regulars, Gallowglass Guards) will “rule the roost.”

The Hidden Room Device Discovered

The Group members discover the “hidden room” device within themselves, a “true reader” that analyzes any part of the world for authenticity. It tells them the world is “still a large part bogus” but well-directioned, with the tide flowing in their favor. If they must withdraw, it will guide them to solid ground.

The Dead Dogs Formed

Norbert Hardcore gathers a small presidium called the “Dead Dogs,” hard men who will fight rear-guard to the end. “Nothing but the very hardest of lines will hold the community.” He warns that if the Group won’t accept “heroic hardness,” he’ll cut them.

Chapter Seven: Reports from the Underground

pp. 90–100

“We are the spies who warn and sound, / And now we’re buried under: / But still we warn from underground / With restless buried thunder.”

Project Can This Be Real

Historical context: the “Outer Winds Area Mirages” have been known for two hundred years. Indian legends give an abrupt beginning: “One day they were seen, and they had not been seen before.” Early observers said they looked “like London with a shine on it.” One hundred investigators are sent to verify Spacious City, returning with conflicting reports.

Tart’s Prison Letter

Tart writes about the “windfall factor”: the world is “too light/buoyant” and moves too easily. Stress engineers know this: one person in five in a maximum throng “is not a person and does not have weight.” She calls her method “Trepidation Journalism,” writing in fear to get her creative juices flowing.

The Cadex Camera

Tart describes the camera invented by Dr. Harold Cadex (now institutionalized). It photographs only “real” things. In the ordinary world, one in four or five people and buildings are missing from photos. In Spacious City, nine out of ten fail to appear, though the ratio improves daily as things become more real.

The Quetch-Quatch Ideogram

Tart’s letter describes the Rolo Group as a small-group-unconscious or closed-group-unconscious. To clarify the concept she recalls a Quetch-Quatch ideogram for the seven-person-group-unconscious: ninety or ninety-one brush strokes depicting seven persons (with an empty place for an absent eighth) sitting on the floor of a cave, dreaming and smoking together with their eyes open. They weave the dream out of pipe-smoke and brain-streamers; the dream accumulates into a woven image of a world-city, although the seven dreamers come from a culture with no concept of a city.

Buddy Baumgarden Loses the Old World

Tart closes her letter with the news that Buddy Baumgarden, Four-Stripe Sergeant in charge of the “Project Can This Be Real” advance outpost, has lost faith in the old world. He believes it has disappeared from behind him, that his outpost is now floating above a void between two flickering mirages (the Old World that is gone and the New World that failed to be), and that he is the only real person left in the universe. He tries to cry out a warning, but the air no longer carries his voice. Tart hears him: “I knew him a little bit, both of us being in the queer investigative work.”

Chapter Eight: The Turn of the Tide

pp. 101–113

“And he answered and said: he that dips his hand with me into the bowl, he is the one.” (Matthew)

Norbert’s Warning at the Cherry Bowl

Norbert Hardcore tells Rolo that “a strong swimmer rejoices when the tide begins to turn against him.” When Rolo refuses (“I will not allow the idea of it to become even problematical around here”), Norbert dips his hand into Rolo’s bowl of cherries beside Rolo’s, then crushes and breaks Rolo’s hand and wrist as a Judas-symbol warning (“I dip my hand with yours into the bowl because it’s a symbol”). Rolo, magic enough to heal himself, refuses to. Norbert overturns his chair and leaves the Courts and the Hanging Gardens of Pleasure. “This broke the Group.”

The Broken Circle

The Group examines the damage to their “true read” hidden-room device. When Norbert defected he tore his idioplasm out of the thing, and with it much of the cross-rooting that had entangled all eight members. It is like holding an autopsy on an invisible device known only by implication. The device can still “true read,” but much of its power is gone.

Wolves and Leopards Drama

A drama called “The Wolves and the Leopards” takes over the city at one hundred sites, a sign of “hard times.” It features starving beasts, a leopard eating a child (rubber, officially, but rumor says a real one somewhere), and dances representing refugees on Calamity Day. Political parties called the Wolves and the Leopards are born from the drama, dedicated to fighting each other for “the bones of Spacious City” and already given to “vulture politics.”

Consortium Intrusion

Several hundred representatives of the Expansion and Projection Corporations enter Spacious City as the Consortium. Their arrival accompanies the Wolves and Leopards drama and the seizure of the city’s oracles. An oracle demands a child for the Leopards, Wolves, and Consortium to eat, identifying that child in every case as Rolo.

The Mutual Adoration

Rolo shows his third face when he welcomes the Consortium. After a coin toss over precedence, the men adore him; then he adores them as the mammon of wealth. His declaration “This is our hour, and the power of darkness” is followed by “Mutuality is the thing.” His worshippers try to explain the reversal as holy deception (Ch. 8, pp. 108–109).

The Seven Rugged Dreamers

At Felicity’s gathering of Splendid Mediocrities, Eustace Garroway asks about the seven open-eyed dreamers everyone seems suddenly aware of: when Nelly Mercury plays her bagpipes, she is playing “Seven Rugged Dreamers, a Long, Long Time Ago”; when Brendan sets up his snuff he uses seven small piles “in honor of the seven dreamers.” A nephomantis or cloud-oracle tells Eustace that all the clouds come from the dreamers’ pipes, and there are now more clouds in the world than ever before; they form faster than they can disperse and cannot rise high because of the lowered “Fortean Ceiling.” The Fortean World, the low-air world, is “really the attic or coenaculum of that funny house” whose underground holds most of the rest.

Felicity’s Keystone

Felicity declares she must become the “funny-shaped stone” or keystone to hold the operation together. “Is that not the way it goes in scripture — ‘The funny-shaped stone will become the keystone’?” She hosts her Splendid Mediocrities on the Hanging Gardens, admiring flamboyant heroes for “a quarter of an hour a day.”

Chapter Nine: Is the City Built and the Lord Has Not Built It?

pp. 114–130

Title source: Psalm 127:1 (Vulgate 126:1), on the Lord building the house and guarding the city. The chapter opens with dialogue about the darkened sun and missing moon.

The Collapse Begins

Hornblende says the experience has eroded his grasp on reality and asks whether the world passes the Aquinas test of wholeness, harmony, and radiance. He also applies his own test of elegance and concludes that the creation fails. Rolo predicts a broken kite-string and a fall in flames.

Olympians and Titans

Three impact studies assess the world-change. O’Mardin minimizes its significance; Avram Maniple describes the Group as Olympians and the Consortium as their Titan enemies; Bunko, Kvikmand, and Goblin recast the conflict as human arrogance and uncorrected science. The narrator calls all three estimates correct.

Rolo’s Confession

Rolo admits he wants to be “the boy who sold the world,” unloading a world with a rickety sky at a new-world price. “We’re whipped, not by the Consortium but by the length of our tether.” He says the Group members are “fragments of fractured persons” he dismembered and scattered through his worlds.

The Meanings of SHINE

The dictionary-style entry on p. 126 ranges over brightness, a mirage or projection, a fraud, a pile of gold coins, a smell or stench, and other senses. The entry comes immediately before the collapse.

The Bright Night of Long Knives

At nightfall of the twenty-ninth day, the city collapses into rampage. Wolves and Leopards militias fight indiscriminately. Signboards reading “Rolo is the beast of Revelations” and “Rolo is the Antichrist” appear in the streets, and their bearers are burned at the stake, crucified, hanged-and-drawn, or torn apart by wild horses. A shuffling old man mumbles “to deceive, if possible, even the elect,” and bright young fellows with tongs cut his tongue out. People who begin to ask, “Have we been asleep or have we been mad?” are everted as well. Pre-dawn brings a sky-fall of live snakes instead of manna and quails; the people skin and eat them with gusto: “It is our real father who has sent them to us.”

Chapter Ten: Retreat through Bogus

pp. 131–145

Opening, p. 131: the retreat begins on the thirtieth morning.

The Hover-Craft Shrine

Rolo’s worshippers have turned the hover-craft into a flower-covered shrine. Axes, bolos, flame-throwers, and Rolo’s commands free it. The cult asks him to leave blood from a creature killed in great pain as a token until he returns. He agrees, and Brendan is killed to supply the blood.

Evisceration of Brendan

To provide the requested liter of blood, Rolo asks for “a peasant,” and the strong young people, knowing his mind, bring him Brendan Michaels. Hornblende protests (“He is my father and no farmer”); Felicity offers herself in his place. Rolo refuses: “He has always had very much of the peasant in him. And I will not be needing the magic-mathematics of Farmer Brendan now.” Rolo opens Brendan with hot iron knives, while helpers spread the openings with hot iron tongs. Followers catch more than a liter of the blood as a totem object to keep through “the hidden years.” Brendan dies but does not howl. “Rolo did not have quite the measure of pleasure he intended.”

SNUFF Reports the Antic

SNUFF calls the event a comic group hallucination or dream-town syndrome and compares Brendan’s death with Judas’s. A Minority Exception rejects this account: “It is a pre-vision of hell itself. It is not funny.” It treats the disaster as a warning of something greater in approximately twenty years. The world responds with laughter.

Rejected at Wittenberg

The hover-craft retraces the thirty days and the fifty seconds and returns to the Group’s home base at Wittenberg. (“Out of Wittenberg I will call my son.”) But the hidden-room device tells them the place is “predominantly bogus”: three out of four people in town are wraiths, three out of four buildings mirages. With their “innocent ignorance” lost, they cannot land on bogus ground. They lift away from Wittenberg and fly toward Dresden.

The Dresden Dialogs

Coming low over Dresden, the Group finds it close to landable (out of twenty persons here, perhaps only eleven are bogus) but still too flimsy. From this low hover come the “Dresden Dialogs,” a telepsychic confrontation between Rolo’s Group and the city: ten million words of remarkable quality involving a hundred thousand Dresden voices, all in perhaps half an hour or no time at all. The dialogs are described as a broken covenant and a historical moment; Dresden serves notice that it will dispute Rolo when he returns.

Banned at Munich

At Munich the hidden-room device sounds fraud warnings, but Rolo’s companions recognize the fraud within themselves. The Cardinal-Archbishop rebukes them in Latin and forbids Rolo to land by his authority. The device admits “I lied” and acknowledges the cardinal’s account.

The Rangle-Tangle and Felicity’s Fall

A proprietor of the Hellabrunn Rangle-Tangle Bierstube offers Rolo a part interest for one earthquake-gold coin, gaining the use of his notorious name. Rolo buys into the business. He also offers Felicity as an animation who can be reassembled after a sky-dive. The craft rises another half kilometer and he flings her out. She does not scream. Hornblende dimly recalls a commitment between them.

The Deflated Mountains

From Munich to Bern the Group notices that the mountains of Bavaria and Switzerland are not as massive or tall as they had been. They had been “grossly inflated mountains, puffed up with unreality,” and “much of the great mountain-rising of the modern era hadn’t happened at all.” A nineteenth-century divine had warned against “the adoration of Scenery” as “an abdication of Reality.” The hidden-room device shows them a clearer geological world, less cumbered with “useless rock piles.”

The Device Fails at Bern

At Bern, Beth says the reader is dying because Norbert’s contribution has been withdrawn, Brendan’s killed, and Felicity’s shattered. Rolo claims still to hear it. Boys throw stones; Rolo kills two with lightning. The survivors promise to return in greater strength, and Rolo threatens the same for the whole world.

The Director of Twelve Museums

The Director of the Twelve Museums of Bern regards Rolo with “half loathing and half distaste.” He rejects Rolo as an exhibit and takes the lifeless Hornblende as The Elegant Man. Tart steals Hornblende later that day, but he is recovered and returned to display. The passage says the exhibit will stay on display until Rolo’s return in Power and Pleroma, although the novel’s ending does not settle whether Rolo survives.

Milano, Arles, Boulogne

The Group flies from Bern to Milano, and from Milano to Arles, where Nelly Mercury is “left behind in circumstances of sordid horror, to become the material of an anecdote that is told in Hell at the present time.” From Arles they go to Boulogne-on-the-Sea, where Rolo and his last two companions, Chrona Lorngold and Beth Barabbas, realize they have become invisible and inaudible to the people of the town. From Boulogne, the small party goes to “either Spain or England, two very similar lands that are easily confused with each other.”

Chapter Eleven: Till I Come Back

pp. 146–160

Passage, p. 156: “The father would not scrap Rolo. The father was in Rolo, and Rolo was in the father. And who would stop them now?”

The Den-of-Thieves Consensus

Rolo’s vehicle gives out as he enters the den-of-thieves consensus, an assortment of people, proto-people, para-people, principalities, animals, and spirits. He receives shape-, size-, and aspect-changing powers for his adolescence. A superior warns that seeking amusement makes him vulnerable and that replacing him would take a thousand years. Rolo answers with “Before Beelzebub was, I am!”

Chrona Sold, Beth to the Iron Hundred

Chrona objects to Rolo’s new associates and demands he break with them. “What am I to do with such a person?” Rolo asks. “There is always the Market,” one of the den-of-thieves says, “there’s a price to be had for such over-blown effigies.” A man comes and puts a hot iron collar around Chrona’s neck; another brands her left cheek with a hot branding iron. “Rolo, I am your mother!” she cries. “I suppose so,” Rolo replies; “be proud of the price you bring.” Beth holds Rolo to his old promise that she would command a hundred again. Rolo answers, “Aye, an Iron Hundred in Hell.” She accepts. “Report there then.” Beth disappears, even to eyes that can see the invisible. A messenger says a “very important man, very, very important, thrice very important,” wishes to see Rolo. Rolo refuses. He is going into “twenty years or so” of intense leisure and reception: “I go to feed on red-meat thunder.”

Tart’s Battle Report

Tart’s Battle Report, “He can be Had,” says Rolo must be killed before he dens in for his long protected adolescence. Residues of Norbert, Felicity, and Hornblende give her access to his hidden-room device. She plans to implant a false memory of Hornblende praising the Green Groben Frog, exploiting Rolo’s appetite for elegance. Her boys-only rule applies to this fetish trap; she is also pursuing other methods through the Contract Man and others.

The Contract Man’s Deposition

The Contract Man arranges paid killings and calls himself pious because he targets people he regards as verminous. His dying deposition reports more than a hundred deaths among those who understand the threat. In his own operation, Consortium influence has subverted selected contractors, and a trusted killer has turned against him under Rolo’s spell. He describes Tart as confused about a Green Frog, but her own report shows an intentional plan. He dies after a euphoric injection, wishing instead for pain and an effective warning to the world.

The Ordeal of the Animals

Rolo faces the Ordeal of the Animals in a green valley or pit. The judges are Irish Wolves, Estremadura Lions (leopards), and metallic dragons. Visiting legal theorists have strong friendships with things hellish. Advocates speak in inhuman languages; the beasts destroy the advocates before turning on Rolo.

Judgment and Promise

A leopard strikes Rolo “like striped lightning,” an ox-killing blow that smashes his left arm and shoulder. A second jaw-strike shears off “eight-ninths of the dangle.” The other animals close in and bury him, and out of the murderous growling comes “the ugliest and most defiant laughter ever.” When the animals withdraw, Rolo stands among them “radiant with blood.” They lick him with their rough tongues, “even with their hot iron tongues from which he might not flinch.” “Rolo the Abominable Beast had judged himself and he had compelled the lesser beasts to acknowledge him.” “The father would not scrap Rolo. The father was in Rolo, and Rolo was in the father. And who would stop them now?”

The Five Boys and the Green Frog

Five neighbor boys come together in clattering excitement, having all dreamed the same dream: “Something about a Green Frog.” One cries steadily, one suffers green nausea, three laugh. Tart now possesses the sinew of Rolo’s severed shoulder, which strengthens her access to his mind. She gives Rolo “a thought, and an inkling, and an inclination”: that the Green Groben Frog is the most elegant of creatures. Rolo, between ordeals, decides to live one last fantasy “out of time” and steps into “the experience of perfect green elegance.” The boys walk around a boulder that “had never been there before” and find a bright green frog with “a shine on it such as they had never seen on anything.” One pins it with a forked stick.

The Wet-Brains and the Vote

The Tellurian monitor selects the boys and frog as the world’s most important event. Its observers recognize Rolo and argue over his fate. One says killing him now would prevent his return and probably avert destruction for another canonical thousand years. The boys’ votes shift, and one proposes a coin toss. Tart tries to influence the decision. Neither toss nor verdict is narrated; the final line, in the narrator’s voice, is “Aw, won’t they ever decide it!”

Dramatis Personæ

Rolo N.B. Danovitz
King of Babylon • Putto Hyper-Sapiens • Second Beast of Revelation
Rolo Group

Eleven-year-old prodigy and natural dictator. Named for his grandfathers, Numerology Noonan and the genetic tamperer Rolo Raingold. “Danovitz” marks descent from the tribe of Dan, which patristic tradition associates with Antichrist. His face oscillates between beautiful and ugly; the third face is “intricate with deception.”

Quotations:

“I myself am the Lord of Unreality, and I am without limit. The Other is only the Lord of Reality, and Reality is so small a place!”

“I can keep them from entering, and I will not.”

“Oh, I like to tear people apart and scatter them through my several worlds.”

Function: Rolo’s world-building, deceptions, cruelty, and promise to return identify him as Antichrist. When his cult asks him to leave “token blood” as a memento until he returns, he kills Brendan to supply it (Ch. 10), a parody of the Eucharistic “do this in memory of me.”

Brendan Michaels
Master Mathematician • Magician
Rolo Group

Red-headed mathematician who believes “a mathematician is the same as a magician.” Creates the Enabling Algebras and Seventh Equation. The oldest member of the Group and the most childlike. Dream-projects into fairy tales to retrieve mathematical solutions.

Quotations:

“Every baby is born with the wrinkledness of old age. Every new thing arrives complete with fossils of itself.”

“Is the fabric of time a flicker-fabric? Is it made up of intervals of nothing separated by intervals of something?”

Fate: In Chapter Ten Rolo opens Brendan with hot iron knives while helpers spread the openings with hot iron tongs, to draw a liter of “token blood” for Rolo’s cult to keep through the hidden years. Brendan does not howl. His contribution to the hidden-room device dies with him.

Beth Barabbas
Centurion • Tactician • Executive Officer
Rolo Group

A former centurion who commanded a select Hundred at War College, Beth is the Group’s executive officer and tactician. She recognizes the danger of fighting the Consortium and later diagnoses the dying hidden-room device.

Fate: In Chapter Eleven, Beth holds Rolo to his old promise that she would command a hundred again. Rolo: “Aye, an Iron Hundred in Hell.” Beth accepts (“That will fulfill the promise. That’s what I want”) and disappears, even to eyes that can see the invisible.

Chróna Lorngold
Archaeologist • Mother of Rolo
Rolo Group

Archaeologist, Rolo’s mother, and a product of genetic tampering. Her chthonic court grows corrupt quickly. The Barefoot Barons are her political party; the Red-Faced Regulars and Gallowglass Guards are militias. She compares herself to a lioness whose cub rends the mother’s womb.

Fate: After Chróna objects to his new associates, Rolo has a hot iron collar put around her neck and her left cheek branded. She is taken to be sold at the flesh-and-blood market. He tells his mother to be proud of the price she brings.

Norbert Hardcore
Strong-arm • Images Director • Defector
Rolo Group → Dead Dogs

In charge of images, Norbert favors hardness and hatred as forces of world-building. His Chapter Three memo explains dark shine as the shine of reburied gold; the I-Forget Bird has already used the title phrase in Chapter Two.

Quotations:

“It is the reburied gold that gives the earth its obscure shine, its dark shine, the brightness of the ‘sun within.’”

“A desert is a place where a great lot of hatred has been vented.”

“The only magic in world-building, or in anything else, is truculence.”

Fate: Norbert forms the Dead Dogs in Chapter Six. In Chapter Eight he crushes Rolo’s hand and wrist at the cherry bowl, breaks with the Group, and tears his contribution from the hidden-room device. Tart later reports his brave but clumsy death on the barricades of Spacious City.

Hornblende Michaelson
Elegance • Brendan’s Son
Rolo Group

Brendan’s son, committed to elegance. He and Felicity have a commitment that he later only dimly remembers. In Chapter Nine he applies the Aquinas test and his own standard of elegance to the world. During the retreat he loses his independent voice and will and is left an automaton without real life.

Fate: Taken by the Director of the Twelve Museums of Bern in Chapter Ten as the exhibit “The Elegant Man.” Tart of BAM steals him later that day, but he is recovered and put back on display, where he is to stay “until Rolo returns to the world in Power and Pleroma.”

Nelly Mercury
Synthetic Entities Specialist • Bagpiper
Rolo Group

Nelly has an electric crackle in her speech and a cultivated smile. She believes she created Felicity; BAM suspects Nelly is equally synthetic and somebody else’s spy. She plays “Seven Rugged Dreamers” on her bagpipes. In Chapter Nine she asks “What is the ‘moon’?” and cannot remember it.

Fate: Left behind at Arles in Chapter Ten “in circumstances of sordid horror, to become the material of an anecdote that is told in Hell at the present time.”

Felicity Octave
Keystone • Synthetic Person • BAM Infiltrator
Rolo Group / BAM

Recruited by Nelly Mercury and “synthetic to the core”: “put-together,” “put-on,” with a “very large complement of illusion in her.” She is the “absolutely genial person, as Nelly couldn’t quite be,” though a “derivative naturalness kept cropping up in her.” A BAM infiltrator, she hosts parties for the “Splendid Mediocrities” and declares that she must become the “keystone” or “funny-shaped stone” holding the operation together.

Quotations:

“I have the fear that I am an artificial person and have no business with humans at all.”

“It is as difficult and as vital to make and expand a love as to make and expand a world.”

“We synthetic and plastecene people are top Goths and we are building cathedrals of sorts.”

Fate: Rolo offers Felicity to the Rangle-Tangle proprietor as an animation that can be repaired, then throws her from the hover-craft. She refuses to scream. Tart later uses her surviving residue to access the hidden-room device.

Tart
Monitor • Prophet • Antagonist
BAM

The first BAM monitor encountered, posing as a reporter. Tart writes one Letter from Prison, in which she moves from warning against the project to wanting to see how it works out. In Chapter Eleven she develops the frog trap.

Quotations:

“This isn’t really happening, this isn’t really happening.”

“This is a monkey-shine, this is a damned putto-shine . . . a dark and slimy trick.”

“The City is Built, and the Lord has not Built it!” (inverting Psalm 127)

Fate: In Chapter Eleven Tart has gathered “still-living but last-gasp residues” of Norbert, Felicity, and Hornblende, giving her parallel access to the hidden-room device Rolo believes he holds alone. The Contract Man writes that her mind is “smashed and scattered” by a confusion “whose only name is ‘Something about a Green Frog’”; the green frog is her own plan, the lure she is implanting in Rolo. In the last scene, Tart prays for the coin flip to come up “Kill him! Kill him!”

Art, Bart, Hart, Dart
Cocked Eye BAM Monitors
BAM
The four fellow Cocked Eye Hit Guys from BAM who work alongside Tart. They discuss the Group’s “world-buster” potential and the “hidden room” exception they cannot scan. They arrive moments too early at the world-shift, experience severe time distortion, and are shackled by “exuberant” people when the world flips. Later freed by Rolo as political prisoners. (One memo header gives the longer form “Harta” for Hart.)
Consortium Men
Princes of Wealth and Projection
Consortium
Several hundred representatives of the Expansion and Projection Corporations arrive openly in Chapter Eight. Rolo invites them in and their mutual adoration follows. He later declares that they will act as his vice-roy during his absence. Maniple calls them Titans opposing the Group’s Olympians; the Hobgoblin Report interprets both as human arrogances.
Numerology Noonan
Supreme Illusionist • Seer • Fraud
Tertiary (Historical)

Rolo’s paternal grandfather. Norbert describes three performances at the Rialto Theatre in Prairie Dog Town: Friday night, Saturday matinee, and Saturday night. The apparent forty-eight-hour experience is subsequently said to have taken seven minutes, as part of Noonan’s study of illusion becoming material.

Noonan appears to disembowel a farmer before the audience, then makes the town disappear. The body and the approaching animals still seem to be there. He insists the murder is real, but his taunts leave Norbert uncertain about what he witnessed.

Noonan recalls taking a fifty-dollar gold piece from his dead Romany mother’s eye.

Nathaniel Noonan
Nobelist • Genetic Engineer
Tertiary (Historical)
Rolo’s father and a Nobel laureate in genetic engineering. Numerology Noonan is disappointed that his son lacks the weirdness required for creative illusion.
Rolo Raingold
Genetic Tamperer
Tertiary (Historical)
Rolo’s maternal grandfather. “Noted and award-winning genetic tamperer.” Provides Rolo’s first name.
The Contract Man
Organizer of Contract Killings
Tertiary

The Contract Man arranges paid killings and counts himself among the Pious Contract Men, whose targets he regards as verminous. He acknowledges that the existence of his profession shows how far the world has been compromised.

His deposition (Ch. 11) reports that more than a hundred people who understood the threat have been killed in a single day. He is betrayed by his own assassin, who falls under Rolo’s “corrupt snake eyes” and declares: “All hail, Rolo, our stench and our leader!”

Alembic Nicholas
Cock-nosed Magician
Tertiary
Cock-nosed magician at Brendan’s Court of Magicians. Toys with his own conjured food (a cod-fish omelet, a Red Rum Benedict, a “hot weasel sandwich”), taking one bite of each before voiding them, then orders real food from Happy Harry’s. Argues that there is no privileged reality and that magic draws power from the capacitance between charged realities.
The Cardinal-Archbishop of Munich
Ecclesiastical Authority
Tertiary
Appears in a balloon to block the Group’s landing in Munich. Places a ban against Rolo’s landing, enforceable because he “knows that he can.”
The Director of Twelve Museums
Museum Curator
Tertiary
The Bern director deals in unusual articles. He regards Rolo with “half loathing and half distaste,” rejects him as an exhibit, and takes Hornblende instead as the exhibit “The Elegant Man.”
The I-Forget Bird
Mythical Entity
Tertiary (Metaphysical)
Allegorical creature from O’Crocker’s tales, dwelling in Uaireanta Valley. Holds the answer to the Seventh Equation. Brendan must engage it “on mathematical subjects.”
Dennis O’Day
Fairy Tale Character
Tertiary (Fictional)
The protagonist of O’Crocker’s tale, which Brendan enters in a dream. As the journey develops, the narration blurs what O’Crocker wrote with what Brendan is dreaming into the story.
The Principality-Animal-Spirit
Den-of-Thieves Being
Tertiary (Demonic)
A being in the den-of-thieves company who is neither a person nor a para-person, but principality, animal, and spirit. He warns that Rolo’s amusement makes him vulnerable and that growing a replacement would take a thousand years.
The Five Grubby Boys
Eschatological Agents
Tertiary

Five neighbor boys who share the same dream, “Something about a Green Frog.” One cries steadily, one suffers “green nausea,” three laugh. They discover Rolo trapped as a Green Groben Frog and debate killing him.

Their votes shift: Kill-Let-Kill-Let-Kill, then sides change. One proposes flipping a coin. The novel ends before they decide.

Ben the Calabrian
Bookmaker
Tertiary
An odds-compiler. The wet-brains at the Tellurian Institute ask, “Somebody get on the line and see what items Ben the Calabrian has posted on the struggle.”
Count Emil Cotswold
Essayist
Tertiary (Fictional Authority)
Cited in Arutinov’s “Back-Door of History”: “Whenever a ship turns over, it is the case of these invisible nines all rushing to one side or the other and crowding the rail there.” The Ninth Class capsizes “ships of state.”
Buddy Baumgarden
Four-Stripe Sergeant • Advance Outpost
Tertiary
In charge of the advance outpost of “Project Can This Be Real,” the investigation into the Outer Winds Area mirages. By the end of Tart’s Chapter Seven letter he has lost faith in the old world: he believes it has disappeared from behind him, that his outpost floats above a void between two flickering mirages, and that he is the only real person left in the universe. He tries to cry out a warning, but the air no longer carries his voice.
Marielena Corte
Impact Study Co-author
Tertiary
Co-author of It Isn’t So Great a Thing as That. She compares the world-change to being moved, asleep, from a childhood house to an inherited castle.
Dennis O’Mardin
Impact Study Co-author
Tertiary
Co-author with Marielena Corte and Saul Minuscule of It Isn’t So Great a Thing as That. He discusses uncertain continuity and fading evidence, including the Kingfisher Nineteen probe’s observation of Earth’s disappearance and replacement.
Saul Minuscule
Impact Study Author
Tertiary
The third named co-author of It Isn’t So Great a Thing as That. He speaks within the report, but only Marielena Corte and Dennis O’Mardin sign at its end. In the exchange that follows, the speakers forget what the missing third person refers to (Ch. 9, pp. 116–120).
Happy Harry
Magician-Producer
Tertiary
Provider of the Happy Harry Trencherman Products ordered by Alembic Nicholas. Brendan argues that the food establishes a preferred reality; Alembic answers that Harry is a better magician in food and drink.
The Shuffling Old Man
Prophet
Tertiary
“A shuffling old man was mumbling the old shuffling quotation”: “to deceive, if possible, even the elect.” For this, “bright young fellows, with tongs and cutters, had the tongue out.”
Eustace Garroway
Splendid Mediocrity
Tertiary
One of Felicity’s Splendid Mediocrities. In Chapter Eight he asks about the seven open-eyed dreamers and recounts a cloud-oracle’s explanation of the growing clouds and lowered Fortean ceiling.
Dr. Harold Cadex
Inventor
Tertiary
Inventor of the camera that Tart says photographs only real things. She met him during an incarceration and built a camera from his instructions. His confinement in an institution prompts her remark that he technically no longer exists.
Avram Maniple
Impact Study Author
Tertiary
Lead author of the alarmed impact study It Is So Great a Thing as That. “It is a horrible thing, an evil thing.” Began writing “Observations of the Last Three Days of the World” without knowing why.
Mary Coppersmith
Impact Study Co-author
Tertiary
Co-author of the Maniple impact study, which calls the world-shift a “horrible thing.”
George Uncial
Impact Study Co-author
Tertiary
Co-author of the Maniple impact study. Named for the uncial script (ancient rounded majuscule letters).
Raymond Bunko
Hobgoblin Report Author
Tertiary
Lead author of the dismissive Hobgoblin Report: “Cool it, people, cool it. It’s the same world it always was.”
Karen Kvikmand
Hobgoblin Report Co-author
Tertiary
Co-author, with Raymond Bunko and Curtis H. Goblin, of the Hobgoblin Report, which interprets the catastrophe as familiar human arrogance and uncorrected science.
Curtis H. Goblin
Hobgoblin Report Co-author
Tertiary
Co-author of the Hobgoblin Report. His surname matches the report’s title.
Efraim McSorley
Para-sociologist
Tertiary (Fictional Authority)
“The great para-sociologist Efraim McSorley believed that such sharp outbreaks of gun-fire indicate a malaise of civilization.”
Rev. P. Huchede
Theologian
Tertiary (Real Authority)
The Catholic author of History of Antichrist, quoted by the novel in Chapter Eight, p. 105. The excerpt discusses Antichrist’s probable origin in Dan, Babylonian birth, and education by magicians.
Grobin
Artist
Tertiary
The artist who designed Nelly Mercury’s “cultivated smile”: “In fact it was designed for her by Grobin, and it worked.” The novel calls him a “superb artist.”

Inter-Group Memos

Chapter Three presents a series of “foundation papers,” memos written by Group members before the world-shift. They contain much of the novel’s theological and cosmological speculation. This section also includes Tart’s letter from Chapter Seven and the BAM monitors’ memos from Chapter Four.

Rolo N.B. Danovitz Chapter III

Rolo places himself at the center of the project. Although he was born after “most of the foundation-thought” was worked out, he insists on putting it in his own words. He outlines the two-hundred-million-hectare expansion plan as a “trigger move” that will swing the balance into a new category. He calls making something out of nothing “the original and superior way” and dismisses concerns about public suspicion.

Rolo declares: “I myself am the Lord of Unreality, and I am without limit. The Other is only the Lord of Reality, and Reality is so small a place!”

Creation ex nihilo Lord of Unreality Anti-democratic contempt Illusion vs. Reality
Norbert Hardcore Chapter III

Norbert sets out the novel’s theory of gold. In his account gold “bleeds out of” tectonic fractures caused by struggles between builders and destroyers. All the gold of the world is “spilled gold,” payment left by principalities and powers. California gold was not discovered until 1848 because “it wasn’t there yet in 1748.”

Norbert’s memo connects the title to gold and finance: reburied gold gives the earth its obscure, dark shine and inner brightness, which in his account is visible from Mars. He also says that the secret masters of the world stand behind it and guarantee its bills.

Earthquake gold Dark shine (title origin) Secret masters Builders vs. Destroyers Deserts as hatred
Felicity Octave Chapter III

Felicity opens by quoting Rolo’s position that the Group should “dislike, even hate each other” to generate the polarities and capacitance for a quantum move. She rejects this: “Hate-based mathematics, though usually dynamic, is regressive and shriveling.” She argues that love is required, or at least synthetic substitutes such as officiousness and concern.

She also records a fear about herself: “I have the fear that I am an artificial person and have no business with humans at all.” Her doctors assure her she is “only about average artificial.” The phrase “to deceive, if possible, even the elect” keeps recurring to her, and she cannot place its biblical source.

Hatred vs. Love Synthetic persons Deception of the elect Consciousness/awakening
Brendan Michaels Chapter III

Brendan’s memo, “Of the Ancientness of New Things,” develops a metaphysics of time for world-building. Every new thing arrives “complete with fossils of itself” and is remembered as old at its first appearance. Time may be a “flicker-fabric” of intervals of nothing separated by intervals of something, and “eight different time continuums” might broadcast over the same fabric.

He asks whether forcing consciousness on unconscious world-building processes might make them “sick,” as forcing consciousness on body functions disrupts them.

Flicker-fabric time Ancientness of new things Quanta of time Conscious vs. unconscious
Tart (BAM Monitor) Chapter VII

Tart’s Letter from Prison is presented as “Trepidation Journalism,” writing in fear to get the creative juices flowing. From her underground cell she describes the “windfall factor”: the world is too light and buoyant. She reports that, according to stress engineers, one person in five in a maximum throng “is not a person and does not have weight.”

She describes the Cadex Camera and its inventor (now institutionalized), reports an unreality rate of seven to nine in ten in Spacious City, and condemns the Rolo Group at length: “This is a monkey-shine, this is a damned putto-shine . . . a dark and slimy trick.”

Windfall factor Cadex Camera Putto-shine Trepidation Journalism
BAM Monitor Reports (Art, Bart, Hart, Dart) Chapter IV

The BAM inter-group memos describe the agency’s surveillance methods: brain-wave lifts, dream transparencies, and air-carbons of documents. They identify Felicity Octave as BAM’s infiltrator and ask whether Nelly Mercury, “at least as synthetic,” is spying for someone else.

BAM discovers hidden rooms in the Group that resist scanning. Its Putto Hyper-Sapiens discussion recounts an Italian legend with a Borneo parallel: Putti were made brilliant but short-lived, and some escaped extinction by tampering with numbers and disguising their faces.

Surveillance Hidden room exception Putto classification Italy/Borneo legend

Depositions & Testimonies

Lafferty gives much of the novel’s information in depositions, impact studies, field reports, and dying testimonies. These documents assess the Rolo Group from outside it and record the world’s failure to resist.

Deposition and Death of “The Contract Man”

Chapter XI, printed pp. 152–154

“I do not leave the world willingly at all. I cannot afford to go, and the world cannot afford to have me go. An epidemic of death has today struck those of us (more than a hundred of us so far) who know what thing is going on and what a preemptive opportunity is slipping away from us if we do not extinguish one monstrous little boy today.

“The carriers of this selective death epidemic are unusual. It is that elements in the world are inclined to kill us and guard the enemy. A slow fuse has been lit to the world, and it has many protectors. The Destroyer of the World was born into the world, more than eleven years ago, and will now pass into a new and invulnerable stage unless we can prevent that. The slow fuse to the world will burn for about twenty years, and then it will blow up the world. We can still snuff out that burning fuse with our fingers if we do it today. Tomorrow will be too late (even later today may be too late). A week from tomorrow will certainly be too late.

“There are hundreds of Contract Men in the world, some of whom have much larger operations than I have. And yet I am known as ‘The Contract Man.’ A Contract Man puts out contracts on lives; he takes pay and gives pay to have persons, (objectionable persons, of course), obliterated, killed, blotted out. Ours is not an honorable profession. It is not even honorable to be, as I am, one of the Pious Contract Men who see to the removal only of verminous persons who truly need removing. The fact that there are Contract Men, even Pious Contract Men like myself, means that Rolo the Beast and his father the greater Beast are winning the game. How the world has been compromised and rotted!

“What is this sympathy that our rot-spotted world shows for the monstrous Rolo? How and why does our effecting world wrench reality apart and dart in and out of rationality to reverse the course of things and give every victory to the abominations? How has Rolo won the deep commitment of our world so completely?

“And one of the most trusted killers I ever gave a contract to has turned back on me and killed me. He has done it with a pleasant and euphoric injection, but he has left me no doubt that I am in my hour of death.

“‘I really don’t know why I do it, old master,’ he said. ‘It isn’t like me to violate a contract and do a turn-around. But there is something about that vile little bugger Rolo that gets me. He looks at me with those corrupt snake eyes of his, and I’m lost. Now I am his partisan forever. Down with the World! Burn it up, and then vilify its ashes! All hail, Rolo, our stench and our leader!’”

Analysis

The Contract Man arranges paid killings. His attempt to have Rolo killed belongs, with Tart’s work, to the organized resistance. He reports more than a hundred deaths that day among people who recognize the danger. One of his most trusted killers then kills him and says that something about Rolo has won him over.

The killer says he does not know why he broke the contract: Rolo looks at him “with those corrupt snake eyes of his,” and he is lost. Rolo’s hold on him works below rational choice. The killer calls Rolo vile and in the same speech hails him as “our stench and our leader.”

Tart’s Final Hunt

Chapter XI, printed pp. 150–152

“The world is a ball, and the ball is in the mouth of an Estremadura Lion who is Rolo. This lion can swallow this world-ball forever if he is not made to disgorge it at once, today. And should we say to one speck on the ball ‘It might be dangerous for you to plot for safety: better not do it’?

“But I am fey and death-defiant. On my mother’s side, I had twin grandmothers, so I am a cat with more lives than one.
