“Rolo has his vulnerabilities and weaknesses. I will play on his weakness for shines, for monkey-shines and boy-shines and devil-shines. We will trap him in a shine.

“I track Rolo now by the ‘hidden room’ device that he once shared with other members of the Rolo Group, and now believes that he shares with nobody at all. But he shares it with me.

“I have been tracking Rolo all day by the dead bodies that he leaves behind him. I have gathered up still-living but last-gasp residues of Norbert Hardcore (who died bravely — but Oh so clumsily! — on the barricades of Spacious City), of Felicity Octave who was my friend and simpatica, of the elegant Hornblende Michaelson. By the remnants of these three, I am a partaker of the homing information of the ‘hidden room’ device.”

Analysis

Tart acquires access through the last surviving residues of Norbert, Felicity, and Hornblende. Later, flesh from Rolo’s severed shoulder gives her a more direct channel for the final suggestion. His belief that he holds the device alone makes the intrusion harder for him to recognize.

Her plan uses Rolo’s “weakness for shines”: she will “trap him in a shine.” In practice this is the frog scheme, in which she implants a fabricated Hornblende memory praising the Green Groben Frog and so leads Rolo to take that form.

The Wet-Brains at the Tellurian Institute

Chapter XI, printed pp. 158–160

“Yes, of course the frog is Rolo Danovitz.” . . . “He’s been caught in a miniaturizing experiment and now he is helpless before the little boys. Look at the green frog-eyes of him, popping with hate. He’s been caught in the middle of one of his antics by a clutch of kids and he sure does not like it.”

“What a grotesque little trap it is that Rolo’s taken in! How could he have been conned into turning into so awkward and ugly and undistinguished a little frog? And yet it’s surely in his own shape and style. Rolo was always ‘frog grotesque.’

“If the boys do kill him, there will be no return of Rolo in his glory in a few years. He apes the Other in so many things, but in the life-return he cannot ape. If they finish him now, the world will be saved from its probable destruction for another period, probably for the canonical thousand years again.

“The world has become un-momentous though. It has become unreal. And so it merits a ridiculous fate! So the fate of the world depends on whether five grubby little boys kill a green frog or not. But the world is only a bagatelle, a three-penny bouncing ball. It is of no more importance than the frog itself is.”

Analysis

The Tellurian observers recognize the event’s importance while deriding it. One estimates that killing Rolo would save the world from its probable destruction for another period, probably the canonical thousand years. The phrase “canonical thousand years” refers to the thousand years of Revelation 20.

The observers are divided. Some cry “Kill it!” and others “Let it go! We want it to live and grow up and come back and kill us.” The observer who gives the thousand-year estimate also says that Rolo “apes the Other in so many things, but in the life-return he cannot ape”: if the boys kill him now, he will not come back.

The Five Boys’ Dream

Chapter XI, printed pp. 156–158

“Five young boys had come together that afternoon. There was a disturbance and excitement about them. Their coming together was a clattering experience, though they were neighbors and friends. One of them was crying steadily and resolutely. Another of them was suffering from the green nausea which is akin to sea-sickness in its symptoms and is an expression of shock and loathing. The other three boys were laughing the hardest they had ever laughed in their lives. The five of them had just discovered that they had all dreamed the same ridiculous dream the night before. This was the dream whose only name is ‘Something about a Green Frog.’

“‘It will be fun,’ another of them said. ‘What other bunch gets something like this handed to them? We will play the game that the fate of the world depends on whether we kill the green frog or not. Remember how the dream said we would know if it was true? We look at each other and be sure we are all awake. We are. We walk around the boulder that was never here before. Where did it come from? It is here now. Then we walk around the boulder, and if we see a bright green frog, then it is real. Shall we all try it and see?’

“‘All right,’ they all said. They walked around the boulder that had never been there before. And they saw the bright green frog with a shine on it such as they had never seen on anything.”

Analysis

The five boys have dreamed the same dream, which the narrator calls ridiculous. The dream supplies its own test: if they walk around the boulder that “was never here before” and find a bright green frog, the dream is true. They find the frog, with a shine on it unlike anything they have seen. They take the matter up as a game in which the fate of the world depends on whether they kill the frog.

The novel does not say who sent the dream. Tart’s intervention works through Rolo: she implants a fabricated Hornblende memory praising the Green Groben Frog and so leads him into the form the boys expect to find.

Impact Study: It Isn’t So Great a Thing as That

Dennis O’Mardin, Marielena Corte, Saul Minuscule • Chapter IX

“Let us get on with it (this is Dennis O’Mardin). It is all relative. We seem to remember ourselves as living more than twenty-eight days, but we cannot know whether we lived in another world like this one (we did not live in this world more than twenty-eight days ago, for it was not in existence before that); or whether our earlier memories have no corresponding reality.”

The Kingfisher Nineteen Probe was returning to Earth when “Earth disappeared completely, in every way, by every test of mind or instrument or deduction, for fifty seconds.” Then “another world appeared exactly where Earth should have been, but this other world was not Earth.” Seventeen of the nineteen probe members have died “naturally” in the past twenty-eight days; the records have been lost; the ship has sunk to a thousand meters in the ocean. “Within a week, when I see the words ‘Kingfisher Nineteen’ they will mean nothing to me.”

Analysis

The Kingfisher report describes the world-change from outside the planet. Its evidence disappears as witnesses die, records are lost, and memories fade. O’Mardin’s study nonetheless holds that the change does not matter.

SNUFF Impact and Appraisal Report

Royal Order of SNUFF • Chapter X

“The funniest antic of the season is the group hallucination done to several million person-splinters by the putto-boy Rolo Danovitz. This is comedy of a Special kind. Nothing that we remember has ever been so huge, so rank, so rotten in concept, so comical. We are tempted to ask ‘Why can’t we have projection-dreams like that that sweep up people and dislocate worlds?’ And the answer is that we are not Rolo Danovitz.”

“There is a coherence and consistency to the various reports of the dream-town ramble. All the people are experiencing the same place even when they are not experiencing it in the same way. It would probably be possible to reconstruct the dream-town (a very large city apparently) out of the computerized dream experiences of the from one to three million people who might be involved.”

The report describes Brendan’s death: “Like Judas, he burst open and all his bowels gushed out. His flesh was both cut and burned at the openings. He died in great pain but he did not cry out.” The SNUFF agents (“The People With The Glow”) are getting their legal limit of euphoria pills raised; “what happens in twenty days from now wouldn’t worry me personally.”

Analysis

SNUFF’s official account treats the episode as group hallucination and comedy. Its remarks about raising the agents’ limit of euphoria pills, and its unconcern about what happens in twenty days, show that the agency does not take the danger seriously.

Minority Exception to the SNUFF Report

Anonymous Dissenter • Chapter X

“The horrifying shine of Rolo Danovitz is not a group hallucination or a group dream. It is not any antic or caper. It is a pre-vision of hell itself. It is not funny. It has just been voted the funniest story of the year by the Media Mummers, but it is still not funny. Any project that causes even ten thousand deaths is not funny.”

“The greatest imaginable disaster to the human race is scheduled to come down on us. It is so horrible that it is not permitted to come unless it first sends a warning of itself. It has just done so. The Rolo shine was the warning, and the people refuse to be warned by it.”

“There was nothing wrong with it, except everything. It was all of the wrong shape and substance. It wore a coat of motley, but inside it was hell-red. Spacious City dream-town was the world inside the gullet, and there was no getting out of it.”

“We have our warning. We have approximately twenty years to amend ourselves and our world. And what do we do? We giggle about it a lot, and we snigger a lot.”

Analysis

The minority exception dissents from within SNUFF. The official report treats the event as comedy; the dissenter calls it “a pre-vision of hell itself” and a warning of a disaster about twenty years away, which people “refuse to be warned by.”

Impact Report on the Outer Winds Area Mirages

“Project Can This Be Real?” • Field Progress Report by Buddy Baumgarden, Four-Stripe Sergeant • Chapter VII

“The ‘Outer Winds Area Mirages’ have been known to White Men for more than two hundred years, and Indian Legends of the mirages run back several centuries further. The Indian Legends give an abrupt beginning to the Mirages. ‘One day they were seen, and they had not been seen before’ was the way every Indian account of the mirages began.”

“The Indians called these mirages ‘The Visions of Moving Meadows,’ having nothing else to compare the life and movement of them to. Early White Men said that the mirages looked ‘Like London with a shine on it.’ Later White Men said that the mirages looked more like Philadelphia or New York, but more extensive and brighter and taller. And more shining than the known cities.”

“And so ‘Project Can This Be Real,’ by decision at a meeting of the governors of the project this morning, has sent one hundred investigators to go into the ‘Outer Winds area,’ by foot, by motor car, by small airplane, by helicopter, or by the ‘Royal Musical Railways.’” The reports of those who returned fall into four groups of 25 percent each, and they differ widely: beer cans, weird small extraterrestrials with sheep-sized cattle, an inaccessible city always one step ahead, or a perfectly normal place. Ninety-two of the hundred never returned.

Analysis

“Project Can This Be Real” is the outside world’s attempt to verify what the Rolo Group has done. Its results do not agree: the reports of those who return fall into four contradictory groups, and ninety-two of the hundred investigators do not return. The project’s name asks whether the new world is real, a question the novel puts repeatedly.

Maniple Impact Study: It Is So Great a Thing as That

Avram Maniple, Mary Coppersmith, George Uncial • Chapter IX

“Yes, a world did end just twenty-eight days ago. And the present world did begin just twenty-eight days ago. . . . It is a horrible thing, an evil thing, whether or not an evil thing can ever be called great. And it does matter, infinitely.”

Avram Maniple: “About an hour ago, I (Avram Maniple) began to write a document ‘Observations of the Last Three Days of the World.’ But how did I know that we are into the last three days of the world?”

Analysis

Against O’Mardin’s indifference, Maniple calls the change “a horrible thing, an evil thing” that “does matter, infinitely.” The three studies differ sharply in their response to the danger, but the narrator calls all three, including the Hobgoblin Report, correct in their estimates.

Hobgoblin Report: “It’s the Same World”

Raymond Bunko, Karen Kvikmand, Curtis H. Goblin • Chapter IX

“Cool it, people, cool it. It’s the same world it always was. It’s simply that a new legendary has risen out of the old well.”

“Oh Olympians be damned! Ancient tyranny be damned! Titans be damned! . . . So the world belched briefly, twenty-eight days back. The world has a history of such minor eructations.”

Analysis

The Hobgoblin Report holds that nothing has changed: “It’s the same world it always was.” The narrator counts this report among the correct ones as well. The other two studies are described this way: “The un-alarms of the O’Mardin Impact Study, and the alarms of the Maniple Impact Study are both allegorical responses.”

Glossary of Terms

Enabling Algebras
The mathematical work required for the world-shift. Brendan Michaels must complete the algebras before the shift can occur.
First appearance: Chapter Two
Seventh Equation
The final piece of Brendan’s mathematical magic, solved through dream-projection into O’Crocker’s fairy tale.
First appearance: Chapter Two
Fortean Universe
Rolo’s Chapter Three name for a low-air world susceptible to resolute illusionist influence, below 7,000 meters in his model. In Chapter Eight, Eustace describes the world as an attic or coenaculum beneath a lowered ceiling.
First appearance: Chapter Three
Outer Winds Area
The semi-desert location from which the Group arrives. Source of mirages known to White Men for more than two hundred years. Indian legends say “One day they were seen, and they had not been seen before.”
First appearance: Chapter One
Cocked Eye BAM
“Benevolent Advisory Monitors,” a sub-group of SNUFF that surveys the Rolo Group via brain-waves, dream transparencies, and air-carbons of memos.
First appearance: Chapter One
SNUFF
Superview of Normalized Unitized Fact Forming. Parent organization of BAM. Motto: “We know it before it happens.” Issues the final appraisal labeling the event a “group hallucination.”
First appearance: Chapter One (name); Chapter Four (expanded name)
Hidden Room Device
A “true reader” assembled from contributions by each Group member. Tests the authenticity of the ground, that is, whether it is real enough to support them. When members are lost, their contributions are torn out and the device degrades.
First appearance: Chapter Four (hidden rooms); Chapter Six (collective reader)
Putto Hyper-Sapiens
BAM’s classification for Rolo in Chapter Four. Its account connects his changing faces and extraordinary mentality with a legend of brilliant, short-lived Putti. A few evade their thirtieth-night extinction by tampering with the number system and putting on ugly faces. Maniple’s Chapter Nine report separately describes Rolo as an original bronze statue-boy born in Hephaestus’s furnace. In art, putti are small boy figures, often winged.
First appearance: Chapter Four
Earthquake Gold
Gold that appears during seismic events. Brendan, musing on the Uaireanta Valley fairy tale in Chapter Two, theorizes that “every time that the world increases or explodes significantly, gold pours out of all the new fissures and ruptures and joints. Gold is the lubrication at the faults of the earth . . . the deathless symbol of expansion and renovation.” In Chapter Three, Norbert builds on this, identifying the reburied gold of private vaults as the source of the earth’s “dark shine” visible from Mars. Earthquake gold accompanies every world-shift, and Rolo carries large minted hundred-dollar coins of it on the retreat.
First appearance: Chapter One
Cadex Camera
According to Tart’s Letter from Prison, Dr. Harold Cadex’s camera photographs only real things. In the ordinary world, one person or building in four or five is missing, so about 75–80 percent appears. Initially nine in ten are missing in Spacious City, but more appear as the city accrues reality.
First appearance: Chapter Seven
Spacious City
The new metropolis and popular name for the wider city-state or project called Accrual. Its initial sign lists city population eight, the founding Group, and greater metropolitan population 21,695,543. The city grows rapidly as its people and buildings acquire substance.
First appearance: Chapter One (name); Chapter Five (foundation)
The Ninth Class
The Aoratoi kai Anarithmoi, or Invisible and Uncountable Ones, in the nine-class account attributed to Galen and elaborated by Arutinov. They are loud and gaudy but are overlooked. They make rapid migrations and cultural flowerings possible. Chapter Five speculates that they include more than half the world’s people.
First appearance: Chapter Five
No Dramas
Street plays where an “Idiot Child” spins and selects actors from the crowd. Part of the Sudden Cultural Flowering. Always “intrinsic parts of power grabs.”
First appearance: Chapter Five
Dead Dogs
Norbert’s small presidium of three hard men, formed in Chapter Six before his break with Rolo. Its motto declares a dog unfinished until bloated, rotting, and lying on its back with all four feet in the air.
First appearance: Chapter Six
Seven Rugged Dreamers
The motif first appears in Brendan’s seven snuff piles in Chapter Two, recurs in Tart’s seven-person cave ideogram in Chapter Seven, and is named in Nelly’s tune and Eustace’s discussion in Chapter Eight. A cloud-oracle attributes clouds to the dreamers’ pipes; Selma describes belief in their dreaming of later worlds. The text does not identify them.
First appearance: Chapter Two (seven dreams); Chapter Seven (ideogram); Chapter Eight (named dreamers)
Windfall Factor
The phenomenon that the world is “too light/buoyant.” Stress engineers rely on it: one person in five in a maximum throng “is not a person and does not have weight.”
First appearance: Chapter Seven
Trepidation Journalism
Tart’s name for writing in fear to stimulate her creative juices. Her Letter from Prison moves from alarm to fascination with the Rolo project.
First appearance: Chapter Seven
Lord of Unreality
Rolo’s self-designation in his Chapter Three memo: “I myself am the Lord of Unreality, and I am without limit. The Other is only the Lord of Reality, and Reality is so small a place!”
First appearance: Chapter Three
Westering Illusion
Rolo’s account of a westward projection that expanded the American continent. Its builders lost confidence and the illusion collapsed, leaving deserts and lost cities. He promises to restore and double it. This is part of his Chapter Three theory of expansion.
First appearance: Chapter Three
Wolves and Leopards
A recurring image of the barest level beneath civilization, an old drama, and the names of rival political parties. In the Chapter Eight performances, rubber children are eaten by a leopard, with a rumor that a real child may be substituted. Actual wolves and leopards judge Rolo in Chapter Eleven. Maniple also names Wolf and Leopard constellations.
First appearance: Chapter One (phrase); Chapters Five and Eight (drama); Chapter Eleven (ordeal)
Ordeal of the Animals
The trial Rolo must undergo, judged by Irish Wolves, Estremadura Lions, and snap-jawed metallic dragons. “Hell animals” who have “made covenant with hell.”
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Uaireanta Valley
The changing Sometimes Valley of O’Crocker’s tale, entered by Brendan in a dream. The I-Forget Bird supplies the mathematical solution. Brendan wakes with the equation and a cap whose gold has turned to refuse.
First appearance: Chapter Two
O’Crocker’s Crock of Gold Tales
The book of fairy tales Brendan uses to solve the Seventh Equation. Contains the story of the I-Forget Bird in Uaireanta Valley.
First appearance: Chapter Two
I-Forget Bird
The forgetful rook of O’Crocker’s tales. Brendan meets it in dream-projection to retrieve “open-ended lattices” for his mathematics.
First appearance: Chapter Two
Tachyon-Quakes
Earthquakes that send echoes “about eight hours into the past and eight hours into the future.” The premonitory quakes in Chapter One are echoes of the coming world-shift.
First appearance: Chapter One
Sudden Cultural Flowering (SCF)
The immediate burst of culture in Spacious City: newspapers, Haiku Drawings, Hundred Word Essays, No Dramas. Appears before the buildings arise because “the flowering was the motivating force.”
First appearance: Chapter Five
Hanging Gardens of Pleasure
The great terraced gardens of Spacious City, associated with the Group’s courts and its Olympus imagery. Their greenery may be projected. Several familiar trees in the novel are artificial.
First appearance: Chapter Five
Tower of the People
A live data bank containing life-sized images of all Spacious City citizens on individual file doors. “You would declare that every one of those replicas was alive.”
First appearance: Chapter Five
Splendid Mediocrities
Felicity’s coterie. “All the carnal heroes are dead and ascended. . . We are the Splendid Mediocrities, and we will work out the ways of the world with less fire and more rationality.”
First appearance: Chapter Eight
Consortium
The Expansion and Projection Corporations, whose representatives include proxies, theologians, and hired killers. Named in Chapter Four, they appear openly in Spacious City in Chapter Eight. Maniple identifies them as Titans opposing the Rolo Group’s Olympians; Rolo proposes that they govern during his absence.
First appearance: Chapter Four (named); Chapter Eight (open arrival)
Chthonic
Earthly, subterranean, or associated with the underworld. The term appears in Chapter One; in Chapter Six it describes Chróna’s court of spirits-of-the-earth people, new wealth, politics, and corruption.
First appearance: Chapter One (term); Chapter Six (court)
True Read
The function of the hidden room device: analyzing any part of the world for authenticity. Answers “Is it real enough?” for landing or launching.
First appearance: Chapter Six
Holy Deception
What Rolo’s worshipers call his mutual adoration with the Consortium, in which he falls down before Mammon. “There is a reason for it!”
First appearance: Chapter Eight
Aquinas Test
Hornblende’s Chapter Nine test of wholeness, harmony, and radiance, followed by his own test of elegance. He judges the world to have failed. Aquinas’s Summa Theologiae I, q. 39, a. 8 discusses beauty in terms of integrity or perfection, proportion or harmony, and clarity.
First appearance: Chapter Nine
Dark Shine
The I-Forget Bird first says “dark shine” in Chapter Two. Norbert’s Chapter Three memo gives it a gold-and-expansion meaning; Rolo’s third face bears it in Chapter Eight. The SHINE entry in Chapter Nine, p. 126, includes brightness, projection, fraud, a pile of gold coins, and stench. Tart’s uses of “monkeyshine” move from alarm to fascination and finally to a plan to trap Rolo.
First appearance: Chapter Two (title phrase); Chapter Three (gold theory); Chapter Nine (dictionary)
House of Dan
Rolo’s claimed lineage. The surname Danovitz indicates descent from the tribe of Dan. Some eschatological traditions associate Dan with the Antichrist.
First appearance: Chapter One
Second Beast of Revelations
Rolo’s apocalyptic identity, named explicitly in Chapter Eleven at the start of the Ordeal of the Animals: “Rolo Danovitz, the Second Beast of Revelations, knew that he must undergo a trial named ‘The Ordeal of the Animals.’” The “Beast of Revelations” name also appears earlier on the Antichrist signboards in Chapter Nine and on the Rangle-Tangle Bierstube sign in Chapter Ten (“Rolo Son of Dan, Beast of the Apocalypse, and Very Anti-Christ”).
First appearance: Chapter Nine (signboards); Chapter Eleven (named Second Beast)
Barefoot Barons
Chróna’s political party. Along with her militias (Red-Faced Regulars, Gallowglass Guards), they “rule the roost” in Spacious City.
First appearance: Chapter Six
Dresden Dialogs
Telepsychic communication between the fleeing Rolo Group and Dresden’s people. Ten million words of “remarkable high quality” in a simultaneous confrontation with swords.
First appearance: Chapter Ten
Bogus
A recurring term for inadequate authenticity. The hidden-room reader applies it to Wittenberg and Dresden during the retreat. At Munich the reader admits lying, and the Group recognizes the fraud.
First appearance: Chapter Six (term); Chapter Ten (retreat)
Big Papa
Rolo’s paternal title among the fellahin, who identify the little boy as Big Papa when the new population gathers in Chapter Five.
First appearance: Chapter Five
Iron Hundred
Beth Barabbas’s final assignment. After Rolo promises she will “once more be put in command of a hundred,” she is sent to command “an Iron Hundred in Hell.” Beth considers this the fulfillment of the promise: “That’s what I want.”
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Green Groben Frog
The frog species into which Rolo transforms at the end, “that most elegant of creatures.” He is trapped in this form by five boys with a forked stick. His “little maimed and shriveled forefoot” corresponds to the severed arm he is regenerating.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Frog Magnetism
Rolo’s attempted charm while trapped as a Green Groben Frog. “Oh no no not frog magnetism, there can’t be such a thing. Degauss the stinking thing!” Tart fears he will seduce the boys into releasing him.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Flicker-fabric
Brendan’s Chapter Three question about time: “Is the fabric of time a flicker-fabric? Is it made up of intervals of nothing separated by intervals of something?” He speculates that several time continuums could share the same fabric.
First appearance: Chapter Three
Articulate Ambient
Non-verbal testimony at the Ordeal of the Animals: “the squealing of hot lava pushing itself along with its peculiar ambulation, the grumbling of stone under tectonic strain, the wheezing of metals separating themselves out of ore-rocks at very high heat, the muted ringing of struck limestone pendants in cold caves.”
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Shape-changing/Size-changing/Aspect-changing
Powers Rolo receives upon entering adolescence. “Aspect-changing is, among other things, moving from the invisible to the visible, and back again.” These enable his transformation into the Green Groben Frog.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Den of Thieves
The mixed company Rolo enters in Chapter Eleven, including people, proto-people, para-people, principalities, animals, and spirits. A speaker who is simultaneously principality, animal, and spirit warns him about the risks of his Spacious City adventure.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Tellurian Institute
Research institution with “the finest of everything.” Its monitor “would pick up the most important thing happening in the world at any time.” The “wet-brain-syndrome people” in the Lush Lounge watch the green frog confrontation.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Wet-brain Syndrome
Condition of the Tellurian Institute observers. They “had many things wrong with them, but they had one thing in common with their monitor: they could correctly identify a thing and appraise its importance. They had to have an understanding of the importance of things to be able to deride the big things so expertly.”
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Three-legged Stool
Rolo names magic from Brendan, arrogance from Norbert, and elegance from Hornblende as the three supports needed for the equations. The stool comparison occurs in Chapter Two.
First appearance: Chapter Two
Flesh-and-blood Market
Where Chróna is sold after being branded with a hot iron. “Classic, over-blown, archetypal beauty and chthonic mentality ranks high on the flesh-and-blood market at present.”
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Canonical Thousand Years
The millennial period of Revelation 20. If the boys kill Rolo, “the world will be saved from its probable destruction for another period, probably for the canonical thousand years again.”
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Before Beelzebub was, I am!
Rolo’s blasphemous claim, modeled on Christ’s “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). It asserts his precedence over high demons such as Beelzebub.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Rangle-Tangle Bierstube
A Munich bierstube whose proprietor offers Rolo a part interest for one earthquake-gold coin. Rolo buys the interest, allowing his name to advertise the business. He also offers Felicity as a repairable animation and throws her from the higher-hovering craft.
First appearance: Chapter Ten
Knight of the Empty Seat
Tart coins this name for Norbert in the present hour, Chapter One. Nelly interprets it as meaning that he was absent once, is absent now, or will be absent, and that his absence is his important attribute. Norbert leaves the Group in Chapter Eight.
First appearance: Chapter One
Dog Robber
“It has been said that I was ‘Dog Robber’ for Numerology Noonan; and that I am also a sort of ‘Dog Robber’ for his grandson the Rolo. Well, I do a little bit of dirty work.” Norbert’s role as loyal subordinate who handles unsavory tasks. In every Illusionist-Creationist group, “there is always ‘one Dog Robber, Experienced.’”
First appearance: Chapter One
Happy Harry Trencherman Products
The catering service Alembic Nicholas orders from after sampling his own conjured food. Brendan treats this preference as evidence for a preferred reality; Alembic says Happy Harry is the better magician in food and drink.
First appearance: Chapter Six
Kingfisher Nineteen Space Probe
O’Mardin reports that the returning probe found Earth absent for fifty seconds and then replaced by a different world in the same position. Seventeen of nineteen crew members have since died; records are lost and the craft lies a thousand meters under the sea. The report warns that the survivors’ memory of even the probe’s name is fading.
First appearance: Chapter Nine
Poppycock Snuff
Brendan’s opium-laced snuff. He lays out seven piles in honor of the seven dreams and allows for visitors who may partake.
First appearance: Chapter Two
The Missing Moon
After twenty-eight days, Beth notices they have seen no phase of the moon. Nelly asks what the moon is and says she cannot remember it. The exchange opens Chapter Nine.
First appearance: Chapter Nine
Rubber Children
A novelty dealer supplies one hundred rubber children for the Wolves and Leopards performances. A rumor persists that a live child might be substituted somewhere.
First appearance: Chapter Eight
Calamity Day
A day prophesied in the dramas “when the earth would smoke and the rocks and roads would sizzle.” The day of the refugees in the Wolves and Leopards drama.
First appearance: Chapter Eight
Gallowglass Guards
One of Chróna’s two named militias, alongside the Red-Faced Regulars. The Barefoot Barons are her political party. Her wider political and financial circle has its own banks and currency.
First appearance: Chapter Six
Quetch-Quatch Ideogram
Tart describes a ninety- or ninety-one-stroke ideogram for the seven-person group-unconscious. Seven open-eyed dreamers smoke in a cave, leaving an empty place for an eighth; smoke and brain-streamers form an image of a world-city, although their culture has no concept of a city.
First appearance: Chapter Seven
Red-meat Thunder
“I go to feed on red-meat thunder. I’ll be in my world-sized, ambulatory cocoon for twenty years or so.” Rolo’s description of his planned adolescent hibernation.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Nine Legions
“If he dens in, he will be protected by nine legions of his own kind, and we will not be able to come at him.” Demonic forces that will guard Rolo during his transformation.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Iron-clad
“When he returns, in twenty years or so, he will return as an Iron-clad and he will be very hard to kill.” Rolo’s invulnerable adult form after adolescent transformation.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Dune Buggy
“The grandson of the old hover-craft, the dune buggy vehicle, breathed its last now.” A descendant vehicle that dies at the end of the novel.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Lush Lounge
Where the “wet-brain-syndrome people” at the Tellurian Institute watch the green frog confrontation on their monitor.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Dream-town Syndrome
SNUFF’s dismissive explanation of Spacious City in Chapter Ten. The Minority Exception instead calls the Rolo shine a pre-vision of Hell and a warning of a greater disaster about twenty years ahead.
First appearance: Chapter Ten
Artificial Trees
Hackberry and several other familiar trees are projective or unreal in the novel’s cosmology. Chapter Six’s discussion of city greenery cites Leo Donoghue’s “False Green, False Flesh.”
First appearance: Chapter Five
Spaciousness Unlimited
The Group’s formal name. Their charter states their object: “The Effecting of miracles of expansion and spaciousness, even to the making of new worlds, and turning it all at a profit.”
First appearance: Chapter One
Written on the Standing Air
How Tart’s final battle report is written: on the air rather than on paper. “Air carbons” of memos are also produced.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Brain-wave Lifting
BAM surveillance technique. “BAM techniques allowed the lifting of brain-waves, by wireless device, to a distance of a thousand meters.” Combined with monitoring of blood sugar, adrenalin flow, and breath rhythm.
First appearance: Chapter Four
Veracity Instruments
BAM’s truth-detection technology for verifying the reality of events: “Our veracity instruments show that it is happening.”
First appearance: Chapter Five
Manna-brand Proto-popcorn
Falls from the sky along with quails during the world-shift. “Hot quails and manna-brand proto-popcorn fallen from the sky.” At the collapse, replaced by “a sky-fall of live snakes.”
First appearance: Chapter Five (named food); Chapter Two (white manna-like food)
Unchallenged Excellence
Norbert protests in Chapter Eight: “Unchallenged excellence is an abomination!” He opposes Rolo’s demand that danger be excluded and holds that excellence requires a challenge.
First appearance: Chapter Eight
Proverbial Blind Reeds
“This is the case of the proverbial blind reeds leaning on the other blind reed.” Describes the Group members’ mutual dependence on Rolo for center and balance.
First appearance: Chapter Four
Theogonous Low-level Lightning
A description of the Dresden Dialogs. Theogonous means generating or giving birth to gods.
First appearance: Chapter Ten
Sharper-than-a-Serpent’s-Tooth Jokes
“Several hundred hours of show-stopping witticisms. These were the ‘sharper-than-a-serpent’s-tooth’ jokes. They were quips that challenged belief.” Part of the final-day revel.
First appearance: Chapter Eight
Black Roses, Serpent Flowers, Eternal Flame Blooms
The flowers burying the hover-craft shrine, “with piles of garlic cloves and bunches of ramps arranged in unorder.”
First appearance: Chapter Ten
Para-people
One of the categories named in Chapter Eleven’s den-of-thieves company, alongside people, proto-people, principalities, animals, and spirits.
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Preterhuman
“The disaster has been committed by a long-lived, arrogant, preterhuman group.” Also: “In the upper crust of us humans (or preterhumans) there is an arrogant silliness that would not be tolerated in commoners.” The word means beyond human.
First appearance: Chapter Nine
Olympians
Tart uses Olympian language in Chapter Seven; Rolo’s Olympus appears in Chapter Eight. In Chapter Nine, Maniple identifies the Group with long-lived preterhuman Olympians and the Consortium with Titans. The Hobgoblin Report calls both “only arrogances within ourselves.”
First appearance: Chapter Seven (Olympians); Chapter Eight (Olympus); Chapter Nine (Maniple’s report)
Titans
The Maniple impact study’s name for the Consortium men in Chapter Nine, the “ancient enemies” of the Olympians (the Rolo Group), who reappear in the world. The Maniple study hopes for “another of those titanic battles between the two forces, a battle in which (we hope) both powers are somehow defeated.” The Hobgoblin Report rejects the framing: “The Titans and the Olympians are only arrogances within ourselves.”
First appearance: Chapter Nine
Innovation Killeth
“Innovation killeth, but Constancy giveth life,” a parody of 2 Corinthians 3:6 (“the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life”). The accompanying paradox is that “a new world can be built with sudden competence only if the crawling innovation is ruthlessly suppressed.”
First appearance: Chapter Five
Non-ferrous Magnetics of Gold
Gold’s power to attract bread, shelter, defense, luxury, and entertainment at once.
First appearance: Chapter Five
Anomaly of the Insufficient Weight of Time
“More than one mathematician has come onto the ‘Anomaly of the Insufficient Weight of Time.’ But if eight of such anomalies should be added together, might not the contrareity disappear and the weight of time become sufficient?”
First appearance: Chapter Three
Fellahin
The common people of the new world, described in the royal-court discussion as royal people in disguise. They recognize the Organization and Rolo as Big Papa, and provide a population for the expanding city.
First appearance: Chapter Five
Son of Dan
The Cardinal-Archbishop’s address to Rolo in Chapter Ten. Chapter Eight, p. 105, quotes Rev. P. Huchede on Antichrist’s probable Danite origin. Earlier parallels include Irenaeus, Against Heresies V.30.2, and Hippolytus, On Christ and Antichrist 14–15.
First appearance: Chapter Ten
Twin Grandmothers
Tart’s claim: “On my mother’s side, I had twin grandmothers, so I am a cat with more lives than one.” Having twin grandmothers is “really better than being the seventh daughter of the seventh daughter.”
First appearance: Chapter Eleven
Exacuerunt tamquam gladium linguas suas
“They have whetted their tongues like a sword” (Psalm 64:3). The Cardinal-Archbishop’s Latin rebuke to Rolo’s group for their mockery.
First appearance: Chapter Ten

Cosmology & Ontology

This section sets out the accounts of reality that characters give in Dark Shine: a vertical model assembled from Rolo, Eustace, Tart, and Bart; the kinds of reality the novel distinguishes; gold, weight, and the hatred and love that fuel the project; the mechanics of projection; and anomalies of time.

The Vertical Structure of Reality

Above 7,000 Meters (Rolo’s memo)
Rolo’s Chapter Three memo places the strato-winds and harsh high-altitude weather beyond local illusionist control. He contrasts his mastery of the low-air world with the Other’s dominion over reality.
The Fortean Ceiling (Eustace’s account)
In Chapter Eight, Eustace reports a lowered roof to the inhabitable world. Clouds accumulate beneath it, and echoes are associated with consciousness and wit.
The Low-Air World (Fortean Universe)
The low-air world is susceptible to resolute illusionist influence in Rolo’s model. Eustace calls it an attic or coenaculum and links its clouds to the Seven Dreamers through a cloud-oracle’s report.
The Surface (Tart’s camera account)
Tart says one person or building in four or five is missing from ordinary Cadex photographs, leaving about 75–80 percent visible. In Spacious City nine in ten are missing at first, and more appear as the city gains reality.
Underground (Several recurring images)
Eustace’s house has most of its structure underground. Norbert imagines reburied gold producing the earth’s dark shine; BAM’s prison is underground; Rolo says his father lives below the crust.
Bare Reality (A disputed hypothesis)
Bart’s Chapter Four memo speculates about the barely inhabited real level beneath accumulated illusion. Rolo insists there is a bottom and wants the hidden-room reader to locate it, but the reader proves unreliable. At the end, the narrator insists that the boys and the frog are real and that their decision matters.

Modes of Reality

The “True Read”

Tart’s Cadex Camera photographs only real things. In her account, approximately 75–80 percent of ordinary people and buildings appear, compared with an initial one in ten in Spacious City. The hidden-room reader guides the Group about authenticity, landing, and escape. As members are lost, this collective instrument deteriorates and eventually admits lying.

The Projected/Illusory

Projected forms can accumulate matter and become temporarily real. O’Hanlon’s epigraph to Chapter Five says that hallucination and group hypnosis can create “their own matter,” and Rolo describes seeming expansion becoming reality. Tart’s Cadex photographs record the process: a growing share of Spacious City appears in them.

The Bogus

The hidden-room device rejects Wittenberg and Dresden as insufficiently authentic. At Munich the Group recognizes the fraud within itself, and the reader admits that it has lied and acknowledges the cardinal’s authority.

The Synthetic

Felicity and Nelly are described as synthetic. Nelly believes she created Felicity; BAM has implanted material in Felicity and questions Nelly’s unknown origin or employer. Though synthetic, Felicity argues for real affection and perceives the Group’s danger.

The Economics of Reality

Gold

Gold appears as wealth, as payment, and as a sign of expansion. Brendan speculates about gold released by growing land; Norbert describes reburied gold and secret masters who guarantee the world’s bills. During the retreat, Rolo’s earthquake-gold coin buys him a share in the Rangle-Tangle Bierstube.

The Windfall Factor

In Tart’s Letter from Prison, the windfall factor means the world is lighter than expected. She says that one in five people in a maximum crowd has no weight and that engineers accommodate the discrepancy.

Hatred and Love as Fuel

Rolo believes hatred supplies the polarities and capacitance needed for the project. Felicity calls hate-based mathematics regressive and insists on love, even if synthetic affection must stand in temporarily: “It is as difficult and as vital to make and expand a love as to make and expand a world.”

The Mechanics of Projection

The Enabling Equations

Mathematical formulae that make world-shifting possible. Brendan Michaels, the mathematician-magician, creates them. The Seventh Equation is solved through dream-projection into O’Crocker’s fairy tale.

The Hidden Room Device

A collective “true reader” assembled from each Group member’s idioplasm. As members are lost (Norbert defects, Brendan is killed, Felicity is flung from the craft), their contributions tear out and the device degrades. By the end it is unreliable and lies to Rolo.

The Seven Rugged Dreamers

The motif of seven dreamers recurs in Brendan’s snuff ritual, Tart’s cave ideogram, Eustace’s cloud-oracle, and Selma’s account of a widespread belief that dreamers dream later worlds.

Temporal Anomalies

Flicker-Fabric Time

Brendan asks whether time is a flicker-fabric, with intervals of nothing alternating with intervals of something. He speculates that eight time continuums might share it, filling the gaps and accounting for time’s otherwise insufficient weight.

Tachyon-Quakes

Earthquakes send echoes “about eight hours into the past and eight hours into the future.” The premonitory quakes in Chapter One are temporal echoes of the world-shift to come.

The Ancientness of New Things

Every new thing “arrives complete with fossils of itself and with people remembering it as having been around for a long time.” “If a thing is real, the response on first seeing it is ‘Oh, I’ve seen you before: I’d know you anywhere.’”

Gazetteer of Locations

The Old World

Outer Winds Area Region

The semi-desert region from which the Group returns in Chapter One and where the world-shift occurs. Mirages have been reported there for centuries.

Project “Can This Be Real” has found mirages here lasting more than two hundred years, which has led to speculation that the area’s reality is unstable.

Chapters I, II, III, IV, VII
Prairie Dog Town Town

Tillman County, Oklahoma. Site of Numerology Noonan’s greatest performance, in which he conjured an entire illusory town with buildings and inhabitants. A young Norbert served as his assistant. The Rialto Theatre within the town was the setting for the disemboweling performance.

“The whole town was an illusion then, and all the people in it, huh?” What seemed like forty-eight hours turned out to be seven minutes.

Chapter I (backstory)
Babylon City

Rolo’s birthplace. Among archaeologists and excavators, there is “an elite club named the Babylonians.” When any member has a child, they go to Babylon for the birth and the child is proclaimed King of Babylon. Rolo holds this title as “a valid thing.”

Huchede, quoted in Chapter Eight (p. 105), gives Antichrist a Babylonian birth.

Chapters I, IX
The Rialto Theatre Building

Within Prairie Dog Town. “Much larger and finer inside than outside.” Site of Numerology Noonan’s staged disemboweling, performed so realistically that the audience’s “sinful enjoyment of the horror” turned them into a real mob.

Chapter I (backstory)

The Dream World

Uaireanta Valley Mythical

Accessible through dream-projection via O’Crocker’s tales. Sometimes appears as “dismal swampland,” other times as fertile land with “shining cities.” Contains the I-Forget Bird who holds the answer to the Seventh Equation.

Brendan wakes with the equation and with a cap whose gold has turned to refuse.

Chapter II
Toireasc Mountain Mythical

The mountain Brendan must climb to find the hidden seventh pass into Uaireanta Valley. Dennis O’Day walks “up a winding path” according to O’Crocker’s telling.

Chapter II

Spacious City

Spacious City Metropolis

The initial sign gives the city’s population as eight, the founding Group, and the greater metropolitan area as 21,695,543. Roughly two million inhabitants arrive by the first sundown, and the narrative projects the larger figure for the thirtieth afternoon. Tart reports that initially nine in ten people and structures fail to appear on Cadex photographs; the ratio improves as the city accrues reality.

A metropolis of newspapers, theaters, factions, gardens, and towers appears almost at once. Its geometry and structures begin to unravel at nightfall of the twenty-ninth day (Ch. 9, p. 126).

Chapters V–X
Hanging Gardens District District

Location of the Group’s five-story headquarters. The terraces are “tall stairways to Olympus.” Rolo claims there is a step the Consortium cannot find: “When they miss it, they will fall through space for a day, and days, and half a day.”

Chapters V, VIII, IX
Tower of the People Building

A “live data bank” containing life-sized replicas of every person in the city. The novel leaves open whether the replicas are data or the “originals.”

Chapter V
Municipal Mountain Structure

A municipal climbing mountain with easy and hard faces. A memorial graveyard at its foot commemorates those who died in falls.

Chapter V
Cenotaph of Rolo N.B. Danovitz Monument

Planned as “an equally fine resurrection edifice among the Spacious City Megaliths.” The Pyramids were “Resurrection Geometry,” and Rolo’s cenotaph was to be the modern equivalent.

Chapter V
Court of Magicians Venue

Where Brendan Michaels presides over magicians of Spacious City and debates the cock-nosed Alembic Nicholas about whether there is privileged reality. Alembic toys with conjured food (cod-fish omelet, Red Rum Benedict, hot weasel sandwich) before ordering real food from Happy Harry’s.

Chapter VI

The Retreat

Wittenberg City

The home base of the Rolo Group, fulfilling the prophecy “Out of Wittenberg I will call my son.” First attempted landing after leaving Spacious City. The hidden room device judges it “predominantly bogus” (three out of four people in town are wraiths, three out of four buildings mirages), and the Group’s lost “innocent ignorance” prevents them from landing on bogus ground. They lift away and fly toward Dresden.

Chapter X
Dresden City

The Group hovers near Dresden during a telepsychic confrontation. Ten million words and one hundred thousand voices are recorded, in at most half an hour and perhaps no time. The city serves notice that it will dispute Rolo’s return.

Chapter X
Munich City

At Munich the Cardinal-Archbishop blocks the Group’s landing. The hidden-room device, which had rejected Wittenberg and Dresden as bogus, sounds fraud warnings; the Group recognizes the fraud within itself, and the device finally admits that it has lied. The Rangle-Tangle transaction and Felicity’s fall follow above the city.

Chapter X
Bern City

“The Town of the Bears.” The Group lands in a Bern parkland after Munich. The hidden-room device, broken by the loss of its members, gives no clear advice. Boys pelt the Group with stones; Rolo kills two with lightning. The Director of the Twelve Museums of Bern declines to display Rolo but takes Hornblende as “The Elegant Man.” The survivors continue to Milano, Arles, and Boulogne before Rolo’s later ordeal in a wasteland.

Chapter X

Cosmic Geography

Above 7,000 Meters Zone

In Rolo’s Chapter Three memo, the strato-winds and unremitting weather above 7,000 meters resist local illusionist influence. The limit bounds the low-air world that Rolo claims as his domain, which he contrasts with the Other’s dominion over reality.

Chapter III
The Fortean Universe Zone

Rolo’s memo describes the low-air Fortean Universe as susceptible to illusionist influence. In Chapter Eight, Eustace develops the image of a lowered ceiling, with reality’s inhabited attic or coenaculum above a mostly underground house.

Chapters III, VII, VIII
The Old Country Conceptual

The unspecified origin from which the Ninth Class immigrate into cities. “They come out of the ground. They come out of the hills. They come out of the walls.” May be subterranean, may be another dimension.

Chapter V

Fictional Authorities

Harold Buildingmaster
Worlds Without End
“How might one tell whether a thing grows, if it grows uniformly, and the measuring-sticks grow at the same time, and all its surroundings grow at the same rate? Oh, of course there are ways to tell if it is growing, especially if it begins to grow just a little bit irregularly. But if they build a new world, and no one knows it, has anything been done?”
Epigraph to Chapter Three. It asks how uniform expansion could be detected when the measuring instruments expand with everything else.
Audifax O’Hanlon
“The Solidity of Hysterical Endeavors”
“There is no such thing as absolute hallucination. There is no such thing as ‘mere’ group hypnosis. Both hallucination and group hypnosis are capable of creating their own matter, their nuclei of reality, however thin these should be.”
Epigraph to Chapter Five. It holds that hallucination and group hypnosis produce real matter, however thin.
Arpad Arutinov
“The Back-Door of History”
“Where do the number nines really come from? They come out of the ground. They come out of the hills. They come out of the walls.”
Source of the extended quotation on the Ninth Class, the Aoratoi kai Anarithmoi (“invisible and uncountable”), the people behind all sudden cultural flowerings.
Leo Donoghue
“False Green, False Flesh”
“there are more green acres in cities than there are in the countryside itself, in the total of ruritania.”
The narrator attributes this paradoxical claim to “False Green, False Flesh” in Chapter Six, p. 87, in his account of the city’s extensive, cultivated greenery.
Count Emil Cotswold
Letters (unspecified)
“Whenever a ship turns over, it is the case of these invisible nines all rushing to one side or the other and crowding the rail there.”
Cited within Arutinov: “ships of state turning over” are caused by rapid population shifts of the invisible class.
Carl Effinger
New Algebra of Strictured Vectors
Rolo assigns this text to Brendan before the world-shift. Brendan initially dismisses Effinger as his second-rate disciple, then recognizes substantial progress. The equations have projective and resonant lattice form and parallel Brendan’s work.
O’Crocker
Crock of Gold Tales
Beth assigns this fairy-tale collection with its endings marked out. Brendan enters the tale of Dennis O’Day’s journey up Toireasc Mountain. The narration does not make clear where O’Crocker’s written story ends and Brendan’s additions through dreaming begin.
Albright
Algebras for the Unconscious
Felicity notes that Rolo “simply hasn’t mastered Albright’s Algebras for the Unconscious,” one of his “blank areas.” The book concerns the parts of world-building that Rolo neglects in favor of conscious control.
Ben the Calabrian
Posted Odds/Items
A bookmaker. The wet-brains at the Tellurian Institute ask someone to “see what items Ben the Calabrian has posted on the struggle,” so bets are being taken on the outcome.

Cultural Productions

Spacious City’s “Sudden Cultural Flowering” produces newspapers, art forms, and theatrical traditions within hours of the city’s creation.

Newspapers

Five great metropolitan dailies appear on the first morning of Spacious City, “founded hours or minutes before the city itself, since they had to carry the news of it.”

The Joyful Journal

Newspaper

One of the five founding newspapers.

The Fountain

Newspaper

Publishes Hundred Word Essays on its first page. The first such essay appears here.

The Daily Declarer

Newspaper

One of the five founding newspapers.

The Ram’s Horn

Newspaper

One of the five founding newspapers. The name alludes to the ram’s-horn trumpet of the Bible.

The Morning Rooster

Newspaper

One of the five founding newspapers. Also publishes Hundred Word Essays.

The Evening Trumpet

Newspaper

An old-world newspaper whose Chapter One headline announces the end of the world.

Art Forms

Haiku Drawings

Visual Art

Drawings of “seventeen strokes of a pencil,” corresponding to the seventeen syllables of a haiku. One of the earliest “old-new art forms” of the Sudden Cultural Flowering.

Hundred Word Essays

Literary Form

Essays of exactly one hundred words, appearing on the first page of newspapers. Originated in “a sort of jurisdictional dispute about an hour before press-time that first morning”: essays under one hundred words could only be written by “arts-and-parts people,” and essays over one hundred words only by “essay people.” The essay of exactly one hundred words was the compromise.

Theatrical Traditions

No Dramas

Theater

The No Dramas begin during the first morning’s drama break, at about a hundred construction sites.

Structure: “A No Drama begins with an idiot child being spun around and around, and then pointing at persons in the crowd to come out and be in the drama.” The selected actors play with their eyes closed, in “‘becoming conscious’ dramas.”

The narrator links No Dramas with power grabs and opposition to those grabs. The Wolves and Leopards become political parties through the drama bearing their names.

“The Stone-Cutter’s Daughters”

Drama

A drama performed at a nearby construction site, set amid earthquake gold and expanding rock. It is “happy in a relentless and muscular way.” The thirty-minute play includes countrified borrowings from older theater.

“The Wolves and the Leopards”

Drama

An old drama performed in Chapter Eight and again discussed in Chapter Nine, when Beth recognizes it as the drama of the twenty-ninth day, the world’s penultimate day. Its beasts and its dances of refugees correspond to events of the collapse. The political parties named for it form before Beth identifies the drama.

“Our Father the Two-Headed Boy”

Melodrama

Among “the most popular of those first morning No Dramas.” Based on “the old legend of the Two-Headed Boy, he with the one ugly head and the one beautiful head, he who was head of the two worlds or the two aspects.” The two heads correspond to Rolo’s beautiful and ugly faces.

“The Abomination of Desolation” (descriptor)

Genre Label

A description of the older “Wolves and Leopards” drama: “an eschatological ‘the abomination of desolation’ play, very rough and fearful in parts of it. The only music instruments allowed to accompany old W and L were flutes and cat-growlers.” The phrase comes from Matthew 24:15. In Chapter Ten the preachers at Arles apply it to Rolo: “How can we be so untroubled when the very Abomination of Desolation is in our midst?”

“We are the Spies” (No Drama Lyric)

Song/Poem

“We are the spies who warn and sound, / And now we’re buried under: / But still we warn from underground / With restless buried thunder.”

The quatrain is the epigraph to Chapter Seven, “Reports from the Underground.” Its buried spies who go on warning correspond to the imprisoned BAM monitors.

Courtly Institutions

The Intellectual Firecracker Court

Institution

“To this court there came firecracker minds from every part of Spacious City, genuine savants with a crisp gunpowder smell about them.” The Three Kings of the Moluccas, the Barons of Conshohocken, and the Count of Bergen County were among them.

A national periodical had called Rolo “the boy genius with the firecracker mind.” The narrator corrects this: Rolo had a “punky mind,” with which he lit the fuses of other people’s firecrackers, and he was “the glowing and hot punk.”

Court in Session

Institution

“Court was in session, but this did not mean quite what it might mean in other places. It was like saying that the City or the City-State was in session. The court was more than a court of law. It was the heart of the realm and it permeated the whole culture.”

“Only an absolute court city can be the center of arts and brilliances. The fellahin understand this, for they are always royal people in disguise.”

Sports & Recreation

Royal Red Raiders

Court Bowling Team

One of the court city’s named teams, with its own home ballpark.

Baronial Blue Battlers

Court Bowling Team

A second team with a home ballpark in the court city’s extensive recreational grounds.

Social Classes (per Galen)

The novel cites “Galen” for a nine-tier class system. The ninth class is “The Floating-World People.”

The Nine Classes

Social Structure

1. Chartered Kings. 2. Natural Kings. 3. Artists, Communicators, Bohemians, and Opportunists. 4. Planters. 5. Manufacturers. 6. Merchants. 7. Docile Workers. 8. Non-docile Workers. 9. The Floating-World People, sometimes called the Aoratoi kai Anarithmoi, or the Invisible and Uncountable Ones.

The ninth class provides “incredible population shifts” and is behind “all sudden cultural flowerings, most especially the brilliant, short, and transitory flowerings.”

Entertainment Venues

Killing-a-Minute Johnny’s

Entertainment Venue

An all-night entertainment venue where the name is taken literally: it has a killing a minute.

All-Night Places

Entertainment

The city’s all-night establishments include restaurants, coffee houses, piano bars, watermelon stands, poppycock booths, smoke houses, and wine taverns.

Political Factions

The Wolves

Political Party

One of two parties formed from the “Wolves and Leopards” drama. It exists solely to fight the Leopards “for the bones of Spacious City.” The name connects it with Rolo’s phrase “Down to the Wolves and Leopards,” his term for the barest level beneath civilization (Ch. 2).

The Leopards

Political Party

Counterpart to the Wolves. Rolo’s totem animal is the leopard. The Estremadura Lions (actually leopards) act as “Judgements of the Father” in the Ordeal of the Animals.

The Barefoot Barons

Political Faction

Chróna Lorngold’s political machine. Part of the chthonic court she establishes. Associated with “vulture politics.”

The Red-Faced Regulars

Political Faction

Another faction in Chróna’s sector, part of the corrupt politics that arise with the city.

The Dead Dogs

Hard-Line Presidium

Norbert’s small presidium of three hard men is formed in Chapter Six, before his break with Rolo. Their dead-dog motto insists on resisting until unmistakably finished. Tart later reports that Norbert died bravely but clumsily on the barricades.

Institutions

The Tellurian Institute

Research Institution

Has “the finest of everything.” Its monitor can “pick up the most important thing happening in the world at any time.” The “wet-brain-syndrome people” in the Lush Lounge watch the green frog confrontation, correctly identifying Rolo and debating whether he should be killed.

The Director of Twelve Museums

Individual/Institution

The Bern museum director views Rolo with “half loathing and half distaste” and rejects him as an exhibit. He takes Hornblende, who becomes The Elegant Man in the museum.

Bestiary

This section groups the animals of Dark Shine as judges, totems, omens, mythical creatures, and symbols.

Judgment Animals

Irish Wolf Hell Animal

“Once called the Great European Wolf, and later believed falsely to be extinct.” One of the “Judgements of the Father” in the Ordeal of the Animals. “There is a hairy and unrepentant evil about these great wolves. They are hell animals, and they have made covenant with hell.”

Eyes “sometimes seemed to be those of dead men and sometimes those of devils.”

Chapter XI
Estremadura Lion Hell Animal

“That tawny and lightly striped leopard misnamed the Estremadura Lion is evil in every organ and sinew of him. He is an animate evil-machine designed to devour and murder in slashing and crunching and tearing agony.”

The leopard’s first ox-killing blow smashes Rolo’s arm and shoulder. A second bite shears off eight-ninths of the dangling limb.

Chapter XI
Snap-Jawed Metallic Dragons Mechanism

“Creatures or mechanisms with hot steel jaws vibrant with crushing, tearing and shearing power.” They dispatch advocates “of metal and stone” while the wolves and leopards handle those “of flesh.”

Their tongues are “hot iron tongues from which [Rolo] might not flinch.”

Chapter XI

Totem Animals

Leopard Rolo’s Totem

Rolo’s personal totem. “His totem was the leopard. But he himself was of another movement and was too chubby to be a leopard type. He would have to be King of the Leopards who by law must be of a non-leopard species.”

“I can take leopards though,” Rolo insists. “The time for them is coming.”

Chapters I, VIII, XI
Green Groben Frog Transformation

The frog species into which Rolo transforms. “Oh, that most elegant of creatures, the Green Groben Frog! What would I not give to be a Green Groben Frog, if only for a short moment!”

Rolo is trapped in this form by five boys with a forked stick. He has “a little maimed and shriveled forefoot,” corresponding to his severed arm, that is “regenerating itself.” He attempts “frog magnetism” to charm the boys into releasing him.

Chapter XI

Omen Animals

Quails Sky-Fall

Quails accompany the premonitory disturbances. “Quails from the sky a-fall” is the third line of Chapter One’s four-line epigraph. The Group roasts and eats the fallen birds.

The fall recalls the quail sent in the wilderness (Exodus 16, Numbers 11). At the collapse, promised manna and quails are replaced by “a sky-fall of live snakes.”

Chapters I, II, IX
Snakes Apocalyptic

Replace the promised quails at the collapse: “a sky-fall of live snakes.” The fires during the collapse appear as “wonderful flaming visions of snakes eating themselves” (ouroboros imagery).

Rolo’s eyes are “corrupt snake eyes” that mesmerize his followers.

Chapters IX, XI
Coyotes, Wolves, Wild Dogs Scavengers

In Norbert’s Chapter One memo, coyotes, wolves, and wild dogs approach after Prairie Dog Town disappears. Noonan says they are drawn by the farmer’s body and gore. Norbert is uncertain whether the killing, the body, or even the animals can be trusted as real.

Chapter I (in Norbert’s memo)

Mythical Creatures

I-Forget Bird Dream Entity

Lives in Uaireanta Valley, accessible through O’Crocker’s tales. Holds the answer to the Seventh Equation. Brendan must engage it “on mathematical subjects” to extract the solution.

Its forgetting has counterparts in the new world, where Nelly cannot remember the moon and the new people are unsure who they are.

Chapter II
Lioness Genetic Parable

In Rolo’s Chapter Three memo, Chróna compares herself to a lioness in the story attributed to Aristotle: her sole cub rends the womb at birth. Rolo answers with a numerical joke about a lion population halving each generation.

Chapter III

Symbolic Categories

“Down to the Wolves and Leopards”

Phrase

Rolo’s phrase names the barest level beneath civilization. Even if everything is reduced to that level, he insists, defense against the beasts is still necessary (Ch. 2). Wolves and leopards appear later as a drama, as political parties, and as judges in the final animal ordeal.

Analytical Timeline

A chronology of the novel’s backstory, the fifty-second world-shift, and the city’s collapse beginning on the twenty-ninth night.

Phase 1.0

Backstory and Genealogy

The family histories behind Rolo and the founding of the Rolo Group and BAM.

1.1 The Legacy of Numerology Noonan

Rolo’s paternal grandfather, described as a “supreme illusionist and creator.”

  • The Prairie Dog Town Illusion: Noonan conjured an entire town, buildings and inhabitants, in Tillman County, Oklahoma. What seemed forty-eight hours turned out to be “seven minutes.”
  • Performance and Cruelty: At the Rialto Theatre, Noonan announced his aristocratic right to “disembowel peasants at any time.” The staged brutality was so realistic that the crowd’s “sinful enjoyment of the horror” turned it into a mob. Norbert’s memo finds Noonan’s influence in Rolo.
  • Philosophy of Creation: Noonan viewed creation as an “insane escape act.” He spent his life seeking a device that would “tell for sure the difference between illusion and fact.” The Rolo Group’s “hidden room” device has the same purpose.
  • The Romany Mother: Noonan took a fifty-dollar gold piece from his dead Gypsy mother’s eye and was left with “the glittering, watching eye of a dead Gypsy mother.”

1.2 The Conception and Inheritance of Rolo N.B. Danovitz

Rolo was designed before birth and proclaimed a king at birth.

  • Genetic and Pre-Natal Influences: Chróna Lorngold subjected him to “genetic tampering” and “cloning and back-cloning” before birth, plus intensive pre-natal instruction.
  • Parentage: Mother is Chróna Lorngold (archaeologist). Father is Nathaniel Noonan (Nobel laureate in genetic engineering), a disappointment to Numerology for lacking “creative-illusion” talent.
  • The King of Babylon: Born in Babylon and proclaimed its king. The kingship is called a “valid thing.”

1.3 Formation of the Factions

Entity Background and Purpose
The Rolo Group
(Spaciousness Unlimited)		 Eight individuals aiming to create a new world. Object: “The Effecting of miracles of expansion and spaciousness.” Members: Rolo Danovitz (leader), Brendan Michaels (mathematician), Beth Barabbas (executive officer), Chróna Lorngold (Rolo’s mother), Norbert Hardcore (strong-arm), Hornblende Michaelson, Nelly Mercury (synthetics), Felicity Octave (recruit).
BAM / SNUFF Benevolent Advisory Monitors and parent organization Superview of Normalized Unitized Fact Forming. Motto: “We know it before it happens.” The “Cocked Eye” sub-group monitors brain-waves, dreams, and communications.
Phase 2.0

The Night at the Mansion

On the night before the world-shift, the Group debates and makes its final preparations at the mansion.

2.1 The Arrival and Initial Confrontation

The Rolo Group makes a “gusty arrival” from the semi-desert “Outer Winds Area,” accompanied by supernatural phenomena: “metallic rich-ringing of coins and nuggets” and “explosive whirl of multitudinous quail wings.”

Tart introduces her investigation by insisting that she wants to know everything, then criticizes the Group’s publicity and motives (Ch. 1, p. 1).

Brendan Michaels explains that the “little earthquakes” and falling gold are only “premonitory kicks,” “tachyon-quakes” that are “echoes of themselves, about eight hours into the past and eight hours into the future.”

2.2 The Philosophical Debate on World-Building

  • Brendan’s Proposal: “Literally and really a new world,” better in almost every way. The Group plans to destroy the old world and build another.
  • Beth’s Methodology: “Wakening a world into being.” They will “un-animate all the stones of this world” but salvage “parts of the old axial stand and the gyroscopy.”
  • Norbert’s Opposition: Reveals Tart’s identity and states his own dissent: he wants to preserve the “Illusion of Spontaneity” within the existing world rather than make new worlds.
  • Tart’s Warning: Confirms she is from “Cocked Eye Hit Guys from BAM” and warns theirs is “the most dangerous group yet.”

2.3 Preparations

Rolo directs Brendan to Effinger’s New Algebra of Strictured Vectors without its resolutions. Beth supplies O’Crocker’s Crock of Gold Tales with the endings marked out. Both readings precede the Seventh Equation.

Rolo explains his equations require a “three-legged stool”: “the magic from Brendan, the arrogance from Norbert, and the elegance from Hornblende.”

Phase 3.0

The Seventh Equation and the World-Shift

Brendan’s dream yields the Seventh Equation; the world-shift follows, and the BAM monitors are captured.

3.1 Brendan’s Dream and the Seventh Equation

Guided by O’Crocker’s tales, Brendan enters a dream state and navigates to Toireasc Mountain, finding the hidden seventh pass into Uaireanta Valley, which is sometimes “dismal swampland” and sometimes “shining cities.”

He encounters the “I-Forget Bird,” which holds the answer. He engages the bird on “mathematical subjects” and writes the “true and valid Synthesis Equation” on maple bark.

3.2 Brendan Wakes

Brendan awakens to great noise. His golf cap, filled with gold in the dream, now overflows with “cinders, clinkers, brick-bats, stones, broken pottery, and walnut and hazelnut shells.”

Beth interprets this transmuted residue as success: “Brendan has been into the golden culture.”

3.3 The World Shift and Arrival

The transition occurs within “only fifty seconds,” accompanied by fifty thousand earthquakes. The Group completes its journey by a hover-flight of “no more than fifty seconds,” landing in “strewn wreckage,” all that is left of the destroyed world.

3.4 The Capture of the Monitors

The BAM quintet arrives as the Rolo Group begins its flight. Art says Rolo will land thirty-eight seconds later. In the distorted transition they witness the expansion and are seized by creatures from it.

Phase 4.0

The First Month in Spacious City

The city appears and fills within a day. Norbert breaks with Rolo, the parties form, and the Consortium arrives.

4.1 Day One: Establishment and Proclamations

  • Morning (about 7 a.m.): Spacious City begins to appear.
  • First Residence: Five-story town house in the “Hanging Gardens District.”
  • First Orders: Norbert to gather earthquake gold; Hornblende to “Raise a militia of ten thousand men.”
  • Naming and Population: The new world or project is Accrual, popularly Spacious City. One sign lists city population eight, the founding Group, and greater metropolitan population 21,695,543.
  • Newspapers and No Dramas: Five great metropolitan newspapers appear that morning. No Dramas begin at about a hundred construction sites during the mid-morning break.

4.2 Factions and Norbert’s Break

The “Turn of the Tide”: Norbert tells Rolo “a strong swimmer rejoices when the tide begins to turn against him” and dips his hand into Rolo’s bowl of cherries beside Rolo’s, then crushes and breaks Rolo’s hand and wrist as a Judas-symbol gesture: “I dip my hand with yours into the bowl because it’s a symbol.” Rolo, magic enough to heal himself, refuses to. Norbert overturns his chair and leaves the Group. (Chrona later explains: “I changed it from that flat-bread that Norbert loved to the cherries that he hated. I didn’t believe that he would dip his hand in the bowl then. And without that symbolism, he wouldn’t have left us.”)

“The tide hasn’t necessarily turned,” Brendan Michaels said just to be saying something. But he was wrong. They all knew that the tide had turned.

Rise of Political Factions: The Wolves and Leopards parties arise from the drama of that name and exist solely to fight “for the bones of Spacious City.”

The Consortium: The Consortium appears openly: the representatives, proxies, theologians, and hit men of the great Expansion and Projection Corporations. An oracle decrees that “a child must be given to the ‘Leopards’ to eat . . . to the ‘Wolves’ . . . to the ‘Consortium,’” and in every case the child must be Rolo. In the Mutual Adoration scene, Rolo first offers them “All this I will give you” and they fall down and adore him; then it is his turn, and Rolo falls down and adores the Consortium, “the mammon of wealth.” His worshipers gasp; others explain it as “the holy deception. There is a reason for it!”

Phase 5.0

The Twenty-Ninth Day and the Collapse

At nightfall of the twenty-ninth day, the project begins its collapse into violence and destruction.

5.1 The Drama of the Twenty-Ninth Day and Rolo’s Declaration

Beth recognizes “The Wolves and the Leopards” performance as the drama of the “twenty-ninth day,” the “penultimate day of the world.”

A last debate about the flaws of the creation ends with Rolo’s account of himself:

“Oh, I’m a boy pulling the last shine of his magic childhood. And you things are fractured because I took the pieces on such a bias and cleavage.”

5.2 “The Bright Night of the Long Knives”

The “bubble” bursts, and the city collapses in fire:

  • The city’s geometry collapses and its forms fall inward. The destruction burlesques form, shape, and purpose (Ch. 9, p. 126).
  • Fires erupt as “wonderful flaming visions of snakes eating themselves.”
  • The Wolves and Leopards militias begin a bloody battle and drag people from their homes.

Rolo welcomes the bloodshed: “Norbert will still be the bloody partisan of my cause. . . But my only cause now is the pyrotechnics and the blood.”

5.3 Rolo’s Withdrawal

At “twenty-four-hour midnight,” Tart confronts Rolo: “You have blocked all the exits!”

Rolo announces that he will withdraw, leaving the Consortium as “vice-roy.” He says: “I go to prepare for my real mission. Next time, the real destruction, with real worlds and real people.”

At pre-dawn, promised manna and quails are replaced by “a sky-fall of live snakes.”

Phase 6.0

The Retreat across Europe

The Group escapes the ruined city, kills Brendan for the token blood, and retreats across Europe. The hidden-room device fails as its members are lost.

6.1 The Escape and the Token Blood

On the thirtieth morning the Group frees the hover-craft from its cultic flowers. Followers ask for a token of blood from a being killed in pain. Rolo has Brendan brought forward, rejects Felicity’s offer to replace him, and cuts Brendan open with hot iron knives while helpers use hot iron tongs. The followers collect more than a liter. Brendan dies without howling.

6.2 The Journey through a “Bogus” World

Their collective reader, already damaged by Norbert’s departure, deteriorates further as members are lost.

  • Path: ruins of Spacious City → Wittenberg → Dresden → Munich
  • At Munich the reader sounds fraud warnings, then admits lying; the Group recognizes fraud within itself.
  • The Cardinal-Archbishop of Munich blocks landing: “You cannot land here.”
  • Flying over Bavaria, Rolo throws Felicity Octave from the hover-craft to her death.

6.3 The Final European Stops

In Bern, Beth says the reader is dying as the Group’s contributions are torn out. Rolo kills two boys with lightning after a stoning. The museum director rejects Rolo and takes Hornblende as The Elegant Man. The survivors travel through Milano and Arles, where Nelly is abandoned, to Boulogne, where they are no longer perceptible to the townspeople. The route then leads to either Spain or England, which the narrator deliberately confuses.

Phase 7.0

“Till I Come Back”: The Ordeal and the Frog Trap

In a wasteland that may have an urban underlay, Rolo disposes of Chróna and Beth, undergoes an animal ordeal, and finally enters Tart’s frog trap. The last scene stops at a proposed coin toss.

7.1 The Den-of-Thieves and the Disposal of Chrona and Beth

Rolo receives shape-, size-, and aspect-changing powers as he enters a long adolescence. A superior warns him that seeking amusement exposes him to danger and that replacing him would take a thousand years. Rolo replies, “Before Beelzebub was, I am!” Chróna protests against his associates; a hot iron collar is placed around her neck, her cheek is branded, and she is taken for sale. Beth accepts command of an Iron Hundred in Hell and disappears.

7.2 Tart’s Battle Report and the Contract Man’s Death

Tart’s Battle Report explains how residues of Norbert, Felicity, and Hornblende let her enter Rolo’s hidden-room network. She plans a false memory praising the Green Groben Frog. Meanwhile the dying Contract Man reports more than a hundred deaths among people aware of the danger. His own trusted killer has turned against him.

7.3 The Ordeal of the Animals

Rolo must undergo “The Ordeal of the Animals”; his father is still angry at him for the Spacious City Shine. The trial is held in a deep and pungent green valley (really a sort of pit), with no judge or jury but the savage animals: Irish Wolves, “Estremadura Lions” (properly leopards), and snap-jawed metallic dragons. Several legal theorists from Berlin, London, and New York attend as guests. “All of them had strong friendships for things hellish..” A leopard strikes Rolo “like striped lightning,” an ox-killing blow that smashes his left arm and shoulder; a second jaw-strike shears off “eight-ninths of the dangle.” The other animals close in and bury him, and out of the murderous growling comes “the ugliest and most defiant laughter ever.” When the animals withdraw, Rolo stands “radiant with blood.” They lick him with their rough tongues, “even with their hot iron tongues from which he might not flinch.” “The father would not scrap Rolo. The father was in Rolo, and Rolo was in the father. And who would stop them now?”

7.4 The Five Boys, the Green Frog, and the Proposed Coin Flip

Five boys discover that they shared a dream about a Green Frog. Tart now has flesh from Rolo’s severed shoulder and supplies the thought that lures him into frog form. The boys find him beyond the newly appeared boulder and pin him with a forked stick. The Tellurian Institute watches as their votes shift. A coin toss is proposed; Tart tries to influence it. The novel ends before the toss or verdict: “Aw, won’t they ever decide it!”

Coda

Rolo’s killing of Brendan for the token blood repeats the cruelty of Noonan’s staged disemboweling at the Rialto. The city, built on a crust with “no bottom under it” (Norbert, Ch. 6), lasts twenty-nine days.

The novel ends without deciding the world’s fate. Five boys debate whether to kill a green frog and propose a coin flip. The Tellurian Institute’s monitor identifies the scene as the most important event in the world, and the narration stops before the decision: “Aw, won’t they ever decide it!”
